label: Formal Sciences
summary: Disciplines concerned with formal systems, such as logic, mathematics, and theoretical computer science.

label: Natural Sciences
summary: The study of the physical world through observation and experiment.

label: Life Sciences
summary: The study of living organisms and life processes.

label: Cognitive Sciences
summary: The interdisciplinary study of mind, cognition, and intelligent behavior.

label: Computer and Information Sciences
summary: The study of computation, information, and automated systems.

label: Engineering and Technology
summary: The application of scientific knowledge to design and build practical systems.

label: Medicine and Health
summary: The science and practice of preventing, diagnosing, and treating disease.

label: Social Sciences
summary: The study of human society and social relationships.

label: Humanities
summary: The study of human culture, including philosophy, history, literature, and the arts.

label: Arts and Design
summary: Creative disciplines spanning visual, performing, and applied arts and design.

label: Practical Knowledge
summary: Applied, skill-based, and craft knowledge oriented toward doing.

label: Meta-Knowledge
summary: Knowledge about knowledge: methodology, epistemology, and knowledge organization.

label: Mathematics
summary: The study of structure, quantity, space, and change.

label: Statistics
summary: The discipline of collecting, analyzing, and interpreting data under uncertainty.

label: Computer Science
summary: The study of computation, algorithms, and information processing.

label: Machine Learning
summary: Machine learning is a subfield of computer science defined in Tom Mitchell's 1997 McGraw Hill textbook as "the study of computer algorithms that improve automatically through experience"; Britannica characterizes it as the discipline "concerned with the implementation of computer software that can learn autonomously." Methodological areas covered in Mitchell's textbook include decision tree learning, artificial neural networks, Bayesian learning, instance-based learning, genetic algorithms, and reinforcement learning. The International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), whose 2025 edition was the forty-second, presents research on "all aspects of machine learning used in closely related areas like artificial intelligence, statistics and data science, as well as important application areas such as machine vision, computational biology, speech recognition, and robotics." The Journal of Machine Learning Research (JMLR), established in 2000, "provides an international forum for the electronic and paper publication of high-quality scholarly articles in all areas of machine learning."

label: Physics
summary: The study of matter, energy, and the fundamental forces of nature.

label: Linear Algebra
summary: The branch of mathematics concerning vectors, matrices, and linear transformations.

label: Vector Space
summary: An algebraic structure of vectors closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

label: Bayesian Inference
summary: A method of statistical inference that updates probabilities as evidence is acquired.

label: Probability Theory
summary: The branch of mathematics that studies random phenomena and reasons about the likelihood of uncertain events.

label: Calculus
summary: The branch of mathematics concerned with continuous change, built on derivatives and integrals.

label: Optimization
summary: The study of selecting the best element, such as a minimum or maximum, from a set of feasible alternatives.

label: Random Variable
summary: A quantity whose value depends on the outcome of a random phenomenon.

label: Probability Distribution
summary: A description of how probability is assigned across the possible values of a random variable.

label: Gradient Descent
summary: An iterative optimization method that updates parameters in the direction that most reduces a function's value.

label: Philosophy
summary: Philosophy is an academic discipline that examines fundamental questions about existence, knowledge, value, reason, and language through systematic argument and analysis. Its major branches include metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, logic, and aesthetics, among others. The discipline traces its recorded origins to ancient Greece, though philosophical traditions developed independently across many cultures.

label: Metaphysics
summary: Metaphysics is the branch of philosophy that investigates the fundamental nature of reality, including questions about existence, identity, causation, time, space, and modality. It encompasses ontology (the study of what exists and the categories of being) as well as inquiries into free will, persistence through change, and the relationship between mind and world. Metaphysics is one of the oldest branches of philosophy, with systematic treatments traceable to Aristotle's Metaphysica.

label: Ontology
summary: Ontology is the branch of philosophy concerned with the fundamental nature of being, existence, and reality, examining what kinds of entities exist and how they relate to one another. Central questions include whether abstract objects such as numbers exist independently of minds, what it means for something to persist through time, and how properties relate to the things that bear them. It is often treated as the core of metaphysics, though some philosophers distinguish ontology from metaphysics proper.

label: Epistemology
summary: Epistemology is the branch of philosophy concerned with the nature, sources, and limits of knowledge and justified belief. It investigates questions such as what distinguishes knowledge from mere belief, what the conditions for epistemic justification are, and how skeptical challenges can be met. Along with metaphysics, ethics, and logic, it is one of the central branches of philosophy.

label: Ethics
summary: Ethics is the branch of philosophy that studies moral principles, values, and conduct, asking what is right or wrong, what kind of person one should be, and how societies ought to be organized. It is conventionally divided into metaethics (foundations of moral judgment), normative ethics (theories of right action), and applied ethics (ethics applied to specific domains). Ethics is one of the oldest and most central branches of philosophy.

label: Logic
summary: Logic is the branch of philosophy and formal science that studies the principles of valid inference, argumentation, and proof. It distinguishes between deductive inference (where conclusions follow necessarily from premises) and inductive inference (where conclusions are supported but not necessitated), and investigates formal systems such as propositional logic, predicate logic, and modal logic. Logic has foundational connections to mathematics, linguistics, and computer science.

label: Aesthetics
summary: Aesthetics is the branch of philosophy concerned with the nature of beauty, art, and aesthetic experience, as well as the principles governing judgments of taste. Central questions include what makes something beautiful or sublime, how artworks convey meaning, and whether aesthetic judgments are objective or subjective. The field overlaps substantially with the philosophy of art.

label: Axiology
summary: Axiology, also called value theory, is the philosophical study of value and goodness, primarily concerned with classifying what things are good and with theoretical questions about the nature of value. A central distinction is between intrinsic value (what is good in itself) and instrumental value (what is good as a means); broadly construed, value theory encompasses questions of value across moral, political, and aesthetic philosophy.

label: Philosophy of Mind
summary: Philosophy of mind examines the nature of mental phenomena — including thought, perception, consciousness, and sensory experience — and especially the relation of the mind to the body and to the rest of the physical world. It is closely related to, while methodologically distinct from, empirical psychology and the cognitive sciences.

label: Philosophy of Language
summary: Philosophy of language investigates the nature of language and the relations between language, language users, and the world, including theories of meaning and speech acts. It was a central area of twentieth-century analytic philosophy, with seminal contributions from figures such as Frege, Russell, and Wittgenstein.

label: Philosophy of Science
summary: Philosophy of science studies, from a philosophical perspective, the elements of scientific inquiry, addressing scientific explanation, the confirmation of theories, laws of nature, and scientific realism, as well as the nature of scientific change. The field became a self-conscious, distinct discipline in the early twentieth century, shaped by logical positivism and empiricism and their critics.

label: Philosophy of Mathematics
summary: Philosophy of mathematics examines the nature and foundations of mathematics, including whether mathematical objects exist independently of minds (Platonism), whether they are mental constructions (intuitionism), or whether mathematics is grounded in language and logic (formalism and logicism). The field has close ties to mathematical logic and the foundations of mathematics, including proof theory, model theory, and set theory.

label: Philosophy of Religion
summary: Philosophy of religion is the philosophical examination of religious beliefs, practices, and concepts, including arguments for and against the existence of God, the nature of faith and religious experience, the problem of evil, and the relationship between religion and science. It applies the methods of analytic and continental philosophy to questions that arise within religious traditions or that bear on them. The field has been practiced in Western academic philosophy at least since the medieval period and continues as a major area of inquiry.

label: Philosophy of Law
summary: Philosophy of law (also called jurisprudence) examines the nature of law, legal systems, and legal reasoning, as well as the moral basis of legal authority and obligation. Central questions include what distinguishes law from morality, what justifies legal punishment, and how judges should interpret statutes. The field encompasses both analytical jurisprudence (what law is) and normative jurisprudence (what law ought to be).

label: Political Philosophy
summary: Political philosophy examines the foundations, justification, and critique of political institutions, authority, and power, addressing questions about the nature of the state, justice, liberty, equality, and rights. It encompasses both normative questions (what political arrangements are just) and analytical questions (what political concepts mean). Political philosophy has been practiced since antiquity and overlaps closely with political theory in the social sciences.

label: Philosophy of Action
summary: The philosophy of action studies the nature of human action, agency, and intention. Central questions include what makes something an action — what distinguishes a genuine action from a mere bodily movement — and how intentions and reasons relate to the causes of action.

label: Philosophy of Perception
summary: Philosophy of perception examines the nature and epistemological significance of perceptual experience, asking how the senses provide knowledge of an external world and what the relationship is between the content of perception and physical reality. Central debates concern whether perception involves direct awareness of external objects (direct or naive realism), mental representations (representationalism), or sense-data intermediaries. The field connects closely with epistemology, philosophy of mind, and cognitive science.

label: Philosophy of Technology
summary: Philosophy of technology examines the nature, development, and social implications of technology, as well as the relationship between technology and human life, values, and society. Topics include the nature of technical artifacts, the ethics of emerging technologies, determinism versus shaping views of technology, and the phenomenology of technological experience. The field gained academic recognition in the twentieth century, with contributions from both continental and analytic traditions.

label: Philosophy of Biology
summary: Philosophy of biology examines the concepts, methods, and theories of the biological sciences, including the species problem, teleology and function in biology, and the structure of evolutionary theory. It established itself as a distinct subdiscipline of philosophy in the second half of the twentieth century.

label: Philosophy of Physics
summary: Philosophy of physics examines the concepts, methods, and theories of the physical sciences, with particular attention to quantum mechanics, the nature of space and time, and statistical mechanics. Central questions include the interpretation of quantum mechanics and the meaning of probability and chance in physical theory.

label: Philosophy of Social Science
summary: Philosophy of social science examines the foundations, methods, and explanatory concepts of the social sciences, addressing questions about the nature of social facts, the role of interpretation in social inquiry, and whether social phenomena can be explained by reducing them to individual actions and mental states. Key debates include the dispute between methodological individualism and holism and the question of whether social sciences can achieve the explanatory standards of the natural sciences. The field draws on philosophy of science, philosophy of action, and the history and sociology of science.

label: Bioethics
summary: Bioethics is the branch of applied ethics that studies the philosophical, social, and legal issues arising in medicine and the life sciences. It emerged as a distinct field of study in the early 1960s.

label: Environmental Ethics
summary: Environmental ethics examines the moral relationship between human beings and the natural world, including the value and moral status of non-human species, ecosystems, and the environment's other non-human contents. Central debates concern whether moral consideration should extend beyond sentient creatures to plants, species, or ecosystems, and what obligations follow from these commitments. The field emerged as a distinct academic discipline in the 1970s.

label: Business Ethics
summary: Business ethics applies ethical theories and principles to the practices, institutions, and decisions of commerce and industry, including questions about corporate responsibility, fair dealing, labor rights, environmental obligations, and the ethics of advertising and finance. It overlaps with applied ethics, corporate governance, and law, and draws on normative theories including consequentialism, deontology, and stakeholder theory. The field gained academic recognition in the latter half of the twentieth century.

label: Metaethics
summary: Metaethics examines the foundations and presuppositions of moral discourse, including questions about the ontological status of moral facts, the semantics of moral language, and the epistemology of moral belief. Major positions include moral realism (moral facts exist independently of minds), anti-realism (they do not), and various intermediate views. It is distinguished from normative ethics, which asks what is right or wrong, by its focus on the nature of moral claims themselves.

label: Normative Ethics
summary: Normative ethics is the branch of moral philosophy concerned with developing and evaluating general principles or theories about how one ought to act. The three major theoretical frameworks are consequentialism (which evaluates actions by their outcomes), deontology (which evaluates actions by their conformity to duties or rules), and virtue ethics (which focuses on the character of the moral agent). It is distinguished from metaethics, which examines the foundations of moral claims, and from applied ethics, which addresses specific practical domains.

label: Analytic Philosophy
summary: Analytic philosophy is a tradition in philosophy that emphasizes clarity of argument, logical rigor, and engagement with formal methods, and that developed primarily in the English-speaking world during the twentieth century. It emerged in the early twentieth century through the work of figures including Gottlob Frege, Bertrand Russell, G. E. Moore, and later Ludwig Wittgenstein, and has since become the dominant approach in Anglophone academic philosophy. Core areas include philosophy of language, philosophy of mind, logic, and formal epistemology.

label: Continental Philosophy
summary: Continental philosophy is a tradition in philosophy that developed primarily in continental Europe during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, encompassing movements such as German Idealism, phenomenology, existentialism, and hermeneutics. It is often characterized by engagement with history, culture, and human experience rather than formal methods, and by concern with questions of meaning, subjectivity, and social critique. The label is primarily used in the Anglophone philosophical world to contrast with analytic philosophy.

label: Phenomenology
summary: Phenomenology is a philosophical movement and method that investigates the structure of conscious experience from the first-person perspective, describing how objects and the world are given to consciousness. Founded by Edmund Husserl in the early twentieth century, it was developed further by thinkers including Martin Heidegger, Maurice Merleau-Ponty, and Jean-Paul Sartre, each of whom extended the method in different directions. The movement has influenced philosophy, psychology, psychiatry, and the social sciences.

label: Existentialism
summary: Existentialism is a philosophical movement that places individual existence, freedom, and choice at the center of philosophical inquiry, holding that human beings define their own meaning in a world without inherent purpose. Associated with thinkers including Soren Kierkegaard, Friedrich Nietzsche, Jean-Paul Sartre, Simone de Beauvoir, and Albert Camus, it reached its widest cultural influence in mid-twentieth-century Europe. Core themes include authenticity, anxiety, absurdity, bad faith, and the priority of existence over essence.

label: Pragmatism
summary: Pragmatism is a philosophical tradition that originated in the United States around 1870 and associates the meaning of concepts with their practical consequences. Its classical period is associated with Charles Sanders Peirce, William James, and John Dewey, and the tradition underwent a significant revival beginning in the 1970s with the neopragmatism of Richard Rorty.

label: Ancient Philosophy
summary: Ancient philosophy refers to the philosophical traditions that developed in the ancient Mediterranean world, principally in Greece and Rome, from roughly the 6th century BCE through the late antique period. It includes pre-Socratic cosmology, the Platonic and Aristotelian schools, Hellenistic movements such as Stoicism and Epicureanism, and Neoplatonism. These traditions addressed questions in metaphysics, ethics, logic, and natural philosophy that continue to inform later Western philosophy.

label: Medieval Philosophy
summary: Medieval philosophy covers philosophical thought roughly from 500 to 1500 CE, including the Latin West together with Greek, Arabic, and Hebrew traditions in the Byzantine, Islamic, and Jewish worlds. Recurring problems include divine foreknowledge, the eternity of the world, the soul and its immortality, and the problem of universals. Scholasticism, the disputational method taught in the Christian schools and associated with figures such as Thomas Aquinas and Duns Scotus, shaped philosophical inquiry in the Latin West.

label: Renaissance Philosophy
summary: Renaissance philosophy covers European philosophy from approximately the mid-15th to the early 17th century, a period marked by the recovery of the literary and philosophical classics of Greece and Rome and by the rise of humanism. Dominant currents include humanism, political philosophy, and the philosophy of nature, alongside Platonist revivals and renewed skepticism, often in opposition to Scholastic method. The period forms a transition between medieval and early modern philosophy.

label: Chinese Philosophy
summary: Chinese philosophy encompasses the philosophical traditions that originated and developed in China, including Confucianism, Daoism, Legalism, Mohism, and later Buddhist-influenced schools. Its formative flourishing is associated with the Spring and Autumn (771–476 BCE) and Warring States periods, the era of the “Hundred Schools of Thought”. These traditions give particular weight to ethics, political philosophy, and cosmology.

label: Indian Philosophy
summary: Indian philosophy encompasses the philosophical traditions of the Indian subcontinent, including the orthodox (astika) systems — Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mimamsa, and Vedanta — and unorthodox (nastika) systems such as Buddhism and Jainism. Its roots reach back to the Vedic hymns of the second millennium BCE, and central concepts include the self (atman), karma, liberation (moksha), and the sources of knowledge (pramana).

label: Buddhist Philosophy
summary: Buddhist philosophy encompasses the philosophical traditions that developed within or from Buddhism, originating with the teachings attributed to Siddhartha Gautama (the Buddha), who lived in northern India between the mid-sixth and mid-fourth centuries BCE. Major traditions include Theravada, Madhyamaka, Yogacara, and Zen, which developed distinct philosophical positions on topics such as the nature of the self, consciousness, causation, and the path to liberation. Buddhist philosophy has been active across South, Southeast, East, and Central Asia, and continues as a living tradition studied in both religious and academic contexts.

label: Islamic Philosophy
summary: Islamic philosophy is the philosophical tradition that developed in the Islamic world from around the 9th century CE, combining Aristotelianism and Neoplatonism with ideas introduced through Islam. Prominent figures include al-Kindi, al-Farabi, Ibn Sina (Avicenna), and Ibn Rushd (Averroes), whose works reintroduced Aristotelianism to the Latin West and remained influential in the development of medieval Scholasticism.

label: Jewish Philosophy
summary: Jewish philosophy refers to the philosophical traditions that developed within or in engagement with Jewish religious, textual, and communal life, spanning from the Hellenistic period through the medieval and modern eras. Thinkers including Philo of Alexandria in the Hellenistic period, and Saadia Gaon, Maimonides, and Gersonides in the medieval period, engaged with Greek philosophical thought while addressing the relationship between reason and revelation. Modern Jewish philosophy has engaged with questions of identity, ethics, history, and the philosophy of religion.

label: African Philosophy
summary: African philosophy encompasses the philosophical traditions, arguments, and concepts that have developed in Africa or among people of African descent, including oral traditions, indigenous thought systems, and academic philosophical work. Recognized currents include ethnophilosophy (the study of collective African worldviews), sage philosophy, African communitarian ethics (Ubuntu), and Africana philosophy addressing the experiences of the African diaspora. The field raises foundational questions about the definition of philosophy and the relationship between oral and written traditions.

label: Japanese Philosophy
summary: Japanese philosophy encompasses the philosophical traditions that developed in Japan, including early engagements with Chinese Confucian and Buddhist thought, the Shinto-influenced intellectual traditions, and the modern period of engagement with Western philosophy. The Kyoto School, founded in the early twentieth century by Nishida Kitaro, is the most internationally recognized school of Japanese philosophy, characterized by its synthesis of Western philosophical methods with Buddhist and East Asian concepts. Japanese philosophy has addressed questions of self, nothingness, aesthetics, and ethics across these periods.

label: Korean Philosophy
summary: Korean philosophy encompasses the philosophical traditions that developed in Korea, including Neo-Confucian thought that flourished during the Joseon dynasty (1392-1910), Buddhist philosophical traditions, and modern engagements with Western and contemporary philosophy. A defining debate in Korean Neo-Confucianism is the Four-Seven Debate between Yi Hwang (Toegye) and Yi I (Yulgok) concerning the relationship between moral emotions, principle, and material force. Korean philosophy has also addressed questions of national identity and modernization in the modern period.

label: Latin American Philosophy
summary: Latin American philosophy encompasses the philosophical traditions that developed in Latin America from the colonial period to the present, including scholastic philosophy introduced during Spanish and Portuguese colonization, nineteenth-century positivism, and twentieth-century currents such as liberation philosophy and philosophy of Latin American identity. Liberation philosophy, emerging in the 1970s, critically engaged questions of economic dependence, cultural identity, and the perspectives of marginalized peoples. The field also investigates whether a distinctively Latin American philosophy exists and what its defining characteristics are.

label: Comparative Philosophy
summary: Comparative philosophy is the philosophical practice of examining and comparing concepts, arguments, and problems across distinct philosophical traditions, such as Chinese and Western philosophy. It aims to identify both commonalities and genuine differences between traditions and to address philosophical questions that benefit from cross-cultural perspectives. The field raises methodological questions about whether cross-traditional comparison is possible without presupposing one tradition's frameworks as universal.

label: Philosophy of History
summary: Philosophy of history examines the nature of historical inquiry, the status of historical knowledge, and the meaning or structure of historical processes. It is divided into two areas: speculative philosophy of history (which asks whether history has a direction or goal) and analytical or critical philosophy of history (which examines the logic of historical explanation and the epistemology of historical evidence). The field addresses questions about historical causation, the nature of historical narrative, and the relationship between history and the social sciences.

label: Philosophy of Economics
summary: Philosophy of economics examines the foundations, methods, and assumptions of economic theory, as well as normative questions about economic justice, welfare, and the ethics of market institutions. It addresses whether economic models provide genuine explanations or only instrumentally useful predictions, and investigates concepts such as rationality, preference, utility, and social choice. The field overlaps with political philosophy, decision theory, and the philosophy of the social sciences.

label: Feminist Philosophy
summary: Feminist philosophy applies feminist perspectives to philosophical questions and critically examines how gender and related categories of identity affect philosophical inquiry, knowledge production, and social arrangements. It encompasses feminist epistemology (examining standpoint theory and objectivity), feminist ethics (including care ethics), feminist political philosophy, and feminist critiques of the history of philosophy. The field emerged as a recognized area of academic philosophy in the latter half of the twentieth century.

label: Philosophy of Education
summary: Philosophy of education examines the aims, methods, and foundations of educational practice, as well as the concepts of teaching, learning, and knowledge transmission. It addresses normative questions about what education ought to accomplish and descriptive-analytical questions about what education is. The field draws on ethics, epistemology, political philosophy, and philosophy of mind.

label: Hermeneutics
summary: Hermeneutics is the theory and practice of interpretation, originally concerned with the interpretation of sacred and classical texts and later extended to all understanding of human expression, action, and culture. Friedrich Schleiermacher and Wilhelm Dilthey established hermeneutics as a systematic philosophical discipline in the nineteenth century, and Hans-Georg Gadamer's work in the twentieth century broadened it into a general account of understanding and dialogue. Hermeneutics has influenced literary theory, theology, the social sciences, and jurisprudence.

label: Metaphilosophy
summary: Metaphilosophy (also called philosophy of philosophy) is the inquiry into the nature, aims, and methods of philosophy itself, asking what philosophy is, how it should be done, and what it can achieve. Questions include whether philosophy makes progress, what distinguishes philosophical from scientific or empirical inquiry, and whether philosophical problems are genuine or merely verbal. The term was popularized in the twentieth century, though reflection on the nature of philosophy has a much longer history.

label: Natural Philosophy
summary: Natural philosophy was the systematic study of the natural world by rational and empirical inquiry, practiced from antiquity into the modern era before the emergence of the modern natural sciences as distinct disciplines. It encompassed the bundle of inquiries now designated as the natural sciences, as well as metaphysical questions about the nature of matter, motion, and causation. The term largely ceased to denote an active academic discipline as the individual sciences became institutionally separated.

label: Scholasticism
summary: Scholasticism was the dominant method of philosophical and theological inquiry practiced in the medieval universities of Europe, characterized by systematic commentary on authoritative texts, formal disputation, and the reconciliation of reason with faith. Major scholastic philosophers include Anselm of Canterbury, Peter Abelard, Thomas Aquinas, Duns Scotus, and William of Ockham. The method left a lasting influence on Catholic theology and philosophy, and Thomism in particular experienced revivals into the twentieth century.

label: Philosophy of Psychiatry
summary: Philosophy of psychiatry examines the conceptual, epistemological, and ethical foundations of psychiatric theory and practice, addressing questions about the nature of mental disorder, the validity of psychiatric classification, and the relationship between biological and psychological explanations of mental illness. It has been shaped by debates over whether mental disorders are natural kinds or socially constructed categories, and by the contributions of figures such as Karl Jaspers.

label: Philosophy of Information
summary: Philosophy of information examines the nature, dynamics, and utilization of information, including questions about what information is, how it relates to knowledge and meaning, and the ethical implications of information technologies. Associated with the work of Luciano Floridi, it investigates the concept of information across philosophy, computer science, and communication theory. The field is considered emerging, having developed into a recognized academic subfield primarily in the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries.

label: Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
summary: The ethics of artificial intelligence examines the moral questions raised by the development and deployment of AI systems, including issues of algorithmic fairness, accountability, transparency, privacy, and the long-term risks posed by increasingly capable AI. It draws on normative ethics, political philosophy, and the philosophy of technology to address both near-term applied concerns and foundational questions about the moral status of AI systems. The field developed rapidly as a recognized area of research in the early twenty-first century.

label: Experimental Philosophy
summary: Experimental philosophy is an approach within philosophy that uses empirical methods, including surveys and behavioral experiments, to investigate how non-philosophers reason about philosophical concepts such as knowledge, free will, moral responsibility, and personal identity. It emerged as a recognized movement in the early twenty-first century and has generated debate about the relevance of folk intuitions to philosophical theorizing. The approach is considered emerging and its methodological standing within academic philosophy continues to be discussed.

label: Decision Theory (philosophical)
summary: Decision theory is the philosophical and formal study of rational choice under conditions of uncertainty, risk, and competing values, examining how agents should form and act on preferences given probabilistic beliefs about outcomes. Its core formalism involves expected utility theory, developed in the twentieth century by figures including Frank Ramsey, John von Neumann, and Leonard Savage. This node refers to the philosophical tradition of decision theory (Wikidata Q177571), which addresses normative questions about rationality and connects to ethics, game theory, and the philosophy of action.

label: Critical Theory
summary: Critical theory, in the sense associated with the Frankfurt School (Wikidata Q301751), is an approach to social and cultural analysis that combines philosophical, sociological, and psychoanalytic methods to critique the ideological structures and social conditions that constrain human freedom and rationality. Associated with the Institute for Social Research (founded in Frankfurt in 1923), key figures include Max Horkheimer, Theodor Adorno, Herbert Marcuse, and Jurgen Habermas. The tradition engages with Marxist theory, Enlightenment rationality, and contemporary social critique.

label: Mathematical Logic
summary: Mathematical logic is the branch of mathematics that studies formal systems, the foundations of mathematics, and the nature of mathematical proof using precise symbolic methods. Its principal sub-fields are set theory, model theory, proof theory, and the theory of algorithms (computability theory), which together investigate the consistency and completeness of formal theories, the relationships between syntactic derivability and semantic truth, and the limits of mechanical computation. Mathematical logic has foundational connections to the philosophy of mathematics, theoretical computer science, and linguistics.

label: Algebra
summary: Algebra is the branch of mathematics that studies algebraic structures — sets equipped with one or more binary operations satisfying prescribed axioms — including groups, rings, fields, and modules. Group theory, whose objects are sets with a single associative binary operation closed under inverses, is historically one of the first examples of an abstract algebraic system and served as a model for the restructuring of other mathematical disciplines. Commutative algebra, homological algebra, and the theory of non-associative algebras are among the principal sub-disciplines, with connections to number theory, algebraic geometry, and topology.

label: Number Theory
summary: Number theory is the branch of mathematics concerned with the properties of integers, with particular attention to prime numbers, divisibility, and Diophantine equations. Its principal sub-disciplines include analytic number theory, which applies methods of mathematical analysis; algebraic number theory, which extends the integers to algebraic number fields; additive number theory, which studies representations of integers as sums; and the geometry of numbers, which uses geometric approaches to arithmetic problems. Long considered the purest branch of mathematics, with no direct applications to the real world, number theory gained practical significance when the advent of digital computers and digital communications revealed that it could provide unexpected answers to real-world problems.

label: Geometry
summary: Geometry is the branch of mathematics whose primary subject is spatial relationships, shapes, and properties of figures and bodies. Its principal branches include Euclidean geometry, founded on Euclid's axioms; analytic geometry, which represents geometric objects by algebraic equations using coordinates; projective geometry, which studies properties invariant under projection; differential geometry, which applies calculus to curves, surfaces, and manifolds; non-Euclidean geometries, which replace Euclid's parallel postulate; and algebraic geometry, which investigates varieties defined by polynomial equations. Modern geometry is closely connected with topology, algebra, and analysis.

label: Differential Geometry
summary: Differential geometry is the branch of mathematics that studies the geometry of curves, surfaces, and manifolds using the methods of mathematical analysis. Classical differential geometry investigates the local properties of curves and surfaces in terms of curvature and torsion, employing the Frenet frame for curves and the two fundamental differential forms for surfaces. Modern differential geometry extends these methods to differentiable manifolds, Riemannian geometry, and complex manifolds, and has foundational applications in general relativity and mathematical physics.

label: Algebraic Geometry
summary: Algebraic geometry is the branch of mathematics dealing with geometric objects defined by polynomial equations — classically algebraic curves and varieties — and their properties studied through the interplay of algebra, topology, and complex analysis. The field extends from the study of algebraic curves, classified by genus, to higher-dimensional varieties and, in its modern formulation, to schemes, the framework introduced to give a unified treatment of varieties over arbitrary fields. Arithmetic geometry, which applies the methods of algebraic geometry to the study of integer solutions of polynomial equations, is a major area with connections to number theory.

label: Topology
summary: Topology is the branch of mathematics that studies properties of spaces preserved under continuous deformations — transformations such as bending, twisting, and stretching that do not involve tearing or gluing. It divides into two principal sub-disciplines: general (or point-set) topology, which investigates abstract topological spaces, continuity, compactness, and connectedness; and algebraic topology, which assigns algebraic invariants such as fundamental groups and homology groups to spaces in order to classify them. Differential topology and knot theory are among the other major areas within the field.

label: Algebraic Topology
summary: Algebraic topology is the branch of mathematics that studies topological spaces by associating algebraic invariants to them, with the aim of classifying spaces up to continuous deformation. Its primary tools include homology groups, which were introduced to measure topological features of spaces and originated in Henri Poincaré's 1895 work on polyhedra; homotopy groups, which classify continuous mappings; and cohomology rings, which carry additional algebraic structure dual to homology. The field also encompasses the study of fibre bundles, characteristic classes, and K-theory.

label: Mathematical Analysis
summary: Mathematical analysis is the branch of mathematics in which functions and their generalizations are studied by the method of limits, encompassing differential calculus, integral calculus, and the theory of series. It provides rigorous foundations for understanding continuity, differentiation, and integration of real-valued and more general functions through the concept of limits and infinitesimal methods. Broader branches that grew from this core include real analysis, complex analysis, functional analysis, and harmonic analysis.

label: Complex Analysis
summary: Complex analysis is the branch of mathematics that studies functions of a complex variable, particularly the class of holomorphic (complex-differentiable) and meromorphic functions. Its central results include the Cauchy integral theorem and formula, the Laurent series representation of functions near isolated singularities, and Riemann's mapping theorem for conformal equivalence of simply connected domains. The field has deep connections to harmonic analysis, number theory, and mathematical physics.

label: Functional Analysis
summary: Functional analysis is the branch of mathematics that studies functions and operators on infinite-dimensional spaces, particularly Banach spaces and Hilbert spaces. It investigates linear functionals, bounded and compact linear operators, spectral theory, and Banach algebras, generalising the methods of linear algebra and classical analysis to infinite-dimensional settings. The field has foundational connections to quantum mechanics, partial differential equations, and operator theory.

label: Harmonic Analysis
summary: Harmonic analysis is the branch of mathematics that studies the representation of functions as superpositions of basic waves, using tools such as Fourier series, Fourier transforms, and almost-periodic functions. It encompasses abstract harmonic analysis on locally compact groups as well as classical trigonometric series and approximation by trigonometric polynomials. The field has close connections to complex analysis, functional analysis, probability theory, and the theory of partial differential equations.

label: Differential Equations
summary: Differential equations is the branch of mathematics that studies equations relating an unknown function to its derivatives, covering both ordinary differential equations (ODEs), which involve functions of a single variable, and partial differential equations (PDEs), which involve functions of several variables. The field investigates existence and uniqueness of solutions, qualitative and stability theory, and solution methods including analytical, geometric, and numerical approaches. Differential equations serve as the primary mathematical language for modelling continuous phenomena in physics, engineering, biology, and economics.

label: Partial Differential Equations
summary: Partial differential equations (PDEs) is the branch of mathematics that studies equations involving an unknown function of two or more independent variables and its partial derivatives. The classical classification divides second-order linear PDEs into elliptic equations (such as Laplace's equation), parabolic equations (such as the heat-conduction equation), and hyperbolic equations (such as the wave equation), each admitting distinct solution theories and boundary-value formulations. PDEs are central to mathematical physics and have driven the development of functional analysis, Fourier analysis, and numerical methods.

label: Dynamical Systems
summary: Dynamical systems is the branch of mathematics that studies how systems evolve over time according to deterministic rules, focusing on the qualitative behaviour of trajectories in phase space rather than explicit solution formulas. The field encompasses topological dynamics, ergodic theory, and smooth dynamical systems, investigating concepts such as equilibria, periodic orbits, limit cycles, invariant manifolds, and chaotic behaviour. It has foundational connections to ordinary differential equations, mathematical physics, and probability theory.

label: Combinatorics
summary: Combinatorics is the branch of mathematics devoted to problems of selecting, arranging, and counting elements of finite or discrete systems according to prescribed rules. Its main areas include enumeration (counting configurations using permutations, combinations, and generating functions), design theory (studying block designs and Latin squares), and graph theory, which provides abstract models for relational structures and covers problems such as planar graphs, the four-colour map problem, and Eulerian cycles. Combinatorics has wide cross-connections with probability theory, algebra, number theory, and theoretical computer science.

label: Set Theory
summary: Set theory is the branch of mathematical logic that studies well-defined collections of objects called sets, with particular focus on infinite sets and the foundations of mathematics. The standard axiom system, Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory with the Axiom of Choice (ZFC), formalizes the theory and supports the development of ordinal and cardinal arithmetic, including the transfinite cardinals introduced by Georg Cantor. Central topics include forcing, the technique developed by Paul Cohen to prove independence results such as the independence of the Continuum Hypothesis from ZFC, and the study of large cardinal axioms that extend the standard system.

label: Model Theory
summary: Model theory is the branch of mathematical logic that studies the relationships between formal languages and their interpretations, called models or structures, with emphasis on first-order logic. Its foundational results include the Completeness Theorem and the Compactness Theorem — which states that if every finite subset of a set of first-order sentences has a model then the whole set has a model — and the Löwenheim–Skolem Theorem, which governs the cardinalities of models of first-order theories. Major research areas include the classification of theories by stability, the study of saturated and homogeneous models, and applications to algebra and non-standard analysis.

label: Proof Theory
summary: Proof theory is the branch of mathematical logic that studies mathematical proofs as formal objects by representing them within explicit deductive systems. Its central program, formulated by David Hilbert, aimed to establish the consistency of mathematics by finitary means; Gentzen's subsequent work provided consistency proofs using transfinite ordinals and introduced cut elimination in the sequent calculus, yielding the proof-theoretic ordinal ε₀ for Peano arithmetic. Major areas include ordinal analysis of formal systems, the study of natural deduction and sequent calculi, and the investigation of subsystems of second-order arithmetic.

label: Computability Theory
summary: Computability theory is a branch of mathematical logic and a foundational area of theoretical computer science that studies which mathematical problems can in principle be solved by algorithmic processes, and which cannot. It formalises the notion of effective computation through models such as Turing machines and recursive functions, establishing results including the undecidability of the halting problem, and its methods underlie the study of computational complexity. Because it grew directly from logical investigations by Gödel, Church, and Turing into the foundations of mathematics, it has dual residence as a subfield of mathematical logic and as a cornerstone of theoretical computer science.

label: Category Theory
summary: Category theory is the branch of mathematics that studies mathematical structures and the relationships between them through the unified language of categories, functors, and natural transformations. A category consists of a class of objects and a class of morphisms between them, closed under associative composition and equipped with identity morphisms; functors are structure-preserving maps between categories; and natural transformations are maps between functors. Category theory unifies constructions across algebra, topology, and logic by identifying universal properties shared by seemingly disparate mathematical objects.

label: Numerical Analysis
summary: Numerical analysis is the branch of mathematics that develops and analyzes algorithms for obtaining numerical approximations to the solutions of mathematical problems involving continuous variables. Its main topics include numerical linear algebra, approximation and interpolation theory, numerical integration and differentiation, the solution of differential equations by finite-difference and finite-element methods, and error analysis. The field is foundational to scientific computing and has applications across engineering, physics, economics, and the natural sciences.

label: Mathematical Physics
summary: Mathematical physics is the field concerned with the application of rigorous mathematical methods to problems in physics, sitting at the junction of the two disciplines. According to the Encyclopedia of Mathematics, it occupies 'a special position, both in mathematics and physics,' connecting with physics through the construction and analysis of mathematical models of physical phenomena while simultaneously advancing as a mathematical discipline in its own right. Its methods include differential and integral equations, operator theory, variational methods, and probability theory, with applications spanning classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and quantum mechanics.

label: Applied Mathematics
summary: Applied mathematics is the branch of mathematics concerned with the development and use of mathematical methods to formulate and solve problems arising in the natural sciences, engineering, economics, and other disciplines outside pure mathematics. Its core areas include differential equations, mathematical modelling, numerical analysis, optimisation, probability and statistics, and mathematical physics. Applied mathematics is distinguished from pure mathematics by its orientation toward real-world problem-solving, though the boundary between the two is not sharp and many areas of applied mathematics have generated substantial pure theory.

label: Operations Research
summary: Operations research is the application of scientific methods to decision-making in the management of complex organized systems — in the Encyclopedia of Mathematics' formulation, the construction, elaboration, and application of mathematical models for making optimal decisions. Its characteristic model classes include mathematical programming (linear, convex, discrete, and stochastic), the theory of games, queueing theory, and network problems. Britannica describes a multidisciplinary practice, normally carried out by teams of scientists and engineers drawn from a variety of disciplines and applied to military, governmental, commercial, and industrial processes. The field is cross-listed across parent disciplines: mathematics classifications carry it as a division of their own (MSC 90, UDC 519.8), the Library of Congress files applied mathematics and quantitative methods with industrial engineering under Technology, and EURO and INFORMS organize its professional community.

label: Game Theory
summary: Game theory is a branch of applied mathematics that provides tools for analyzing situations in which multiple decision-makers, called players, make choices whose outcomes depend on the choices of others. According to Britannica, the field was systematically developed by John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern, whose 1944 book 'The Theory of Games and Economic Behavior' established it as a mathematical framework suited to economic analysis; John Nash further advanced the field in the 1950s. Though rooted in mathematics, game theory occupies shared estate with economics and, more recently, computer science, and Britannica explicitly identifies it as a 'branch of applied mathematics' while acknowledging its central role in economic modeling.

label: Information Theory
summary: Information theory is a mathematical theory concerned with the quantification, storage, and reliable transmission of information, originating in Claude Shannon's 1948 work on communication systems at Bell Laboratories. Shannon's framework established the concept of channel capacity and demonstrated that signals can be transmitted near theoretical capacity even in the presence of noise, creating a rigorous foundation that transformed both electrical engineering and mathematics. The Encyclopedia of Mathematics characterizes information theory as 'the branch of applied mathematics and cybernetics,' reflecting its dual roots: it emerged from practical telephone-industry demands yet is built on probability theory and mathematical analysis.

label: Financial Mathematics
summary: Financial mathematics is the field that applies mathematical methods—in particular stochastic calculus, probability theory, and partial differential equations—to problems in finance such as asset pricing, risk management, and the valuation of derivative instruments. The Encyclopedia of Mathematics traces its modern mathematical foundations to Louis Bachelier's 1900 application of Brownian motion to markets and to the 1973 Black-Scholes formula for option pricing, which relies on geometric Brownian motion and self-financing portfolio theory. The field is anchored in applied mathematics while serving the needs of financial practice, and the Bachelier Finance Society describes it as spanning both academic research and industry application in 'the broad field of mathematical finance.'

label: Bayesian Statistics
summary: Bayesian statistics is a paradigm of statistical inference in which unknown parameters are treated as random variables and uncertainty about them is expressed and updated via probability distributions. The framework proceeds by combining a prior distribution encoding existing knowledge with a likelihood derived from observed data to yield a posterior distribution, following Bayes's theorem. The paradigm has its own active research community and has proven especially effective for problems where frequentist approximations are difficult, though it remains philosophically contested because the choice of prior introduces an element of subjectivity.

label: Time Series Analysis
summary: Time series analysis is the branch of statistics concerned with data observed sequentially over time, formally treating such data as realizations of stochastic processes. Core methods include the analysis of stationary processes, spectral decomposition, moving-average models, and forecasting; Robert F. Engle and Clive W. J. Granger developed influential techniques for series exhibiting time-varying volatility and common trends respectively. The field finds application across economics, engineering, meteorology, and the natural sciences wherever measurements are ordered in time.

label: Computational Statistics
summary: Computational statistics is the subfield of statistics at the interface between the statistical and computing sciences, concerned with the use of computers in data modelling, prediction, and analysis, and with statistical concepts deployed in computing science, for example in machine learning and data analytics. Simulation-based techniques such as the Monte-Carlo method, a numerical method based on simulation by random variables, are among its characteristic tools. Dedicated venues such as the journal Statistics and Computing and the American Statistical Association's Section on Statistical Computing anchor the area within statistics.

label: Mathematical Statistics
summary: Mathematical statistics is the branch of mathematics devoted to the study of mathematical methods for the organization, processing, and utilization of statistical data for scientific and practical conclusions. Its core concerns include parameter estimation using unbiased estimators, hypothesis testing, sequential analysis, statistical decision theory, and the design of experiments. The field relies extensively on probability theory, particularly through sampling theory and asymptotic analysis of inference procedures.

label: History of Mathematics
summary: The history of mathematics is the scholarly discipline that investigates the development of mathematical ideas, notations, and practices across cultures and historical periods, from ancient Babylonian and Greek mathematics through the present. It examines how mathematical concepts emerged and were transmitted between civilisations, how notation shaped the progress of ideas, and how individual contributions fit into longer developmental trajectories. The discipline draws on primary sources, contextual historiography, and collaboration with mathematics, philosophy, and the history of science.

label: Mathematics Education
summary: Mathematics education is the field concerned with the teaching and learning of mathematics and with research on them. Its international scientific body, the International Commission on Mathematical Instruction (ICMI), was established in 1908 at the Fourth International Congress of Mathematicians and, reconstituted in 1952, became an official commission of the International Mathematical Union, devoted to the development of mathematics education at all levels. Research in the field, as the journal Educational Studies in Mathematics frames it, deals with methodological, pedagogical/didactical, political, and socio-cultural aspects of the teaching and learning of mathematics; European researchers organize through ERME, established to promote communication, cooperation, and collaboration in mathematics education research. The field is cross-listed: its commission belongs to the mathematicians' union, while the OECD's research classification files educational sciences within the social sciences.

label: Control Theory
summary: Control theory is the science of methods for determining laws to control systems that can be realized by automatic devices, in the Encyclopedia of Mathematics' formulation. A controlled system is a device whose future development, deterministic or stochastic, is determined by its present state and control parameters; Britannica distinguishes open-loop from closed-loop (feedback) control. Principal tools include Lyapunov stability methods, frequency analysis, controllability and observability criteria, and the Pontryagin maximum principle of optimal control, alongside adaptive control and variable-structure systems. The field is cross-listed between mathematics and engineering: the Library of Congress files control theory at QA402.3 within mathematics and control engineering systems at TJ212-225 within mechanical engineering, while IFAC promotes the science and technology of control in all systems, in both theory and application.

label: Mathematical Biology
summary: Mathematical biology is the interdisciplinary field at the interface of mathematics and the life sciences, concerned with the application of mathematical methods—especially differential equations and numerical analysis—to biological phenomena such as population dynamics, enzyme kinetics, epidemiology, and genetics. The Society for Mathematical Biology, founded in 1973, describes its mission as promoting research and education 'at the interface between the mathematical and biological sciences.' The field is distinct from, though overlapping with, computational biology, and has expanded from its classical focus on continuous dynamical models to include modern mathematical approaches in genomics and other areas.

label: Systems Science
summary: Systems science is an interdisciplinary field devoted to the study of complex systems—their structure, behavior, and the principles that govern them across domains that do not fit neatly within a single traditional discipline. The International Society for the Systems Sciences (ISSS), founded in 1954, is one of the oldest organizations dedicated to advancing systems science, cybernetics, and complexity science, and characterizes the field as addressing transdisciplinary problems such as climate change, artificial intelligence, and economic systems. The field draws on mathematics, engineering, biology, and the social sciences to develop general frameworks applicable wherever components interact to produce emergent system-level behavior.

label: Cybernetics
summary: Cybernetics is the scientific study of control, communication, and feedback in animals, machines, and organizations; the Encyclopedia of Mathematics describes it as the science of “the control, communication and processing of information.” The field was founded by the mathematician Norbert Wiener with his 1948 work Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine, which proposed that feedback and self-regulation operate by common principles across biological and mechanical systems. From the 1960s onward much of its original program differentiated into control theory, systems science, and computer science, yet the field remains institutionally active: the American Society for Cybernetics and the IEEE Systems, Man, and Cybernetics Society continue to operate, dedicated journals including Kybernetes, IEEE Transactions on Cybernetics, and Biological Cybernetics are publishing as of 2026, and degree programs run at institutions such as NTNU (Engineering Cybernetics) and the ANU School of Cybernetics, founded in 2021.

label: Applied Statistics
summary: Applied statistics is the application-facing branch of statistics concerned with using statistical methods to analyze data arising in scientific, industrial, governmental, and social contexts. Its toolkit spans regression and correlation analysis, multivariate methods, experimental design, and survival analysis, and the field spans 'an enormous range from direct subject-matter collaborations to pure mathematical theory' as characterized by the Institute of Mathematical Statistics. Applied statistics draws on the theoretical apparatus of mathematical statistics and deploys it across domains such as healthcare, biology, engineering, education, and economics.

label: Algorithms and Data Structures
summary: Algorithms and data structures is the area of computer science concerned with the design and analysis of step-by-step computational procedures and the methods of organizing data on which they operate. The Encyclopedia of Mathematics defines an algorithm as "detailed instructions defining a computational process" that begins with an arbitrary input and proceeds by "consecutive conversion of constructive objects by discrete 'steps'," producing a result "fully determined by the input"; it also notes that the process "may also terminate without a result being obtained…or may not terminate at all." The word derives from the Latin transliteration of the name of the 9th-century mathematician al-Khwarizmi, and the modern theory of algorithms rests on twentieth-century formalizations by Turing, Post, Markov, and Kolmogorov together with the Church–Turing thesis.

label: Computational Complexity Theory
summary: Computational complexity theory is the branch of theoretical computer science that classifies decidable problems by the resources their solution requires. The Encyclopedia of Mathematics frames it as "a finer classification of decidable problems in terms of their complexity," asking whether one algorithm is better than another "in the sense that it uses fewer resources, such as time or memory space," where time is measured by the number of steps and space by the number of tape squares visited. Central objects of study are complexity classes such as P, the languages accepted by polynomially bounded Turing machines, and NP, those accepted by non-deterministic polynomially bounded Turing machines, together with the NP-complete problems that are "the hardest problems in NP." Whether every NP problem is in fact a P problem—the P versus NP question—was named a Millennium Prize Problem in 2000.

label: Programming Languages
summary: Programming language theory is the branch of computer science concerned with the design, semantics, implementation, and analysis of programming languages. Carnegie Mellon University's Computer Science Department characterizes the area as "a comprehensive science of programming that encompasses not only language design and implementation as ordinarily conceived, but also specification, verification, implementation, evaluation, and validation of programs." The University of Oxford, where "programming language research…began in 1965 with the Programming Research Group," likewise places "work in programming language theory, design and implementation" at the theme's center, spanning topics from functional programming and game semantics to algebra of programming.

label: Software Engineering
summary: Software engineering is the discipline concerned with the systematic application of engineering principles to the specification, design, development, testing, and maintenance of software systems. Britannica defines it as "the discipline concerned with the application of theory, knowledge, and practice to building reliable software systems that satisfy the computing requirements of customers and users," applicable to small-, medium-, and large-scale systems. Britannica also notes that Margaret Hamilton is credited with creating the term "software engineer" to describe her professional work, which included writing code for the command and lunar modules of NASA's Apollo program in the late 1960s and early 1970s. ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology (TOSEM), publishing since 1992, covers "specification, design, development and maintenance" and the tools, methodologies, languages, data structures, and algorithms involved in building large, complex software systems.

label: Computer Networks
summary: Computer networks is the subfield of computer science concerned with the interconnection of computing devices for the purpose of communicating and sharing data. Britannica defines a computer network as "two or more computers that are connected to each other to communicate data electronically," with network architectures standardized under frameworks including the ISO Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model and IBM's Systems Network Architecture (SNA). ACM SIGCOMM — described as "ACM's professional forum for the discussion of topics in the field of communications and computer networks" — covers the technical design and engineering, regulation, operations, and social implications of computer networking, with particular emphasis on systems engineering and architectural questions.

label: Artificial Intelligence
summary: Artificial intelligence is, in Britannica's definition, "the ability of a digital computer or computer-controlled robot to perform tasks commonly associated with intelligent beings," and the term denotes developing systems with intellectual processes characteristic of humans, including reasoning, generalization, and learning from experience. Britannica frames its core abilities as learning, reasoning, problem-solving, perception, and language use, and contrasts rote learning (memorization) with generalization (applying past experience to new situations). Digital computers have been programmed since the 1940s to carry out increasingly complex tasks, and Britannica notes that while some systems match human expert performance on specific tasks, no current program achieves full human flexibility across broader domains.

label: Computer Vision
summary: Computer vision is defined by Britannica as a "field of artificial intelligence in which programs attempt to identify objects represented in digitized images provided by cameras, thus enabling computers to 'see.'" According to Britannica, contemporary methods use "deep learning and neural networks to help computers process visual information," giving a computer "a large data set of visual images" from which it identifies features and patterns that it can then apply to other images. Britannica relates the field to pattern recognition and notes applications including facial recognition and augmented reality.

label: Natural Language Processing
summary: Natural language processing is, in Britannica's definition, "the use of operations, systems, and technologies that allow computers to process and respond to written and spoken language in a way that mirrors human ability," achieved by combining computational linguistics, statistics, machine learning, and deep-learning models. Britannica describes a progression from early systems that were "hand-coded and rule-based" and struggled with nuances such as sarcasm and idiom, to statistical approaches using probability, and then to modern deep-learning systems that learn while processing information. It lists applications including voice-operated navigation, customer-service chatbots, machine translation, and search auto-completion, and notes that bias inherited from training data is a recognized concern.

label: Human-Computer Interaction
summary: Human-computer interaction (HCI) is, in Britannica's definition, "concerned with designing effective interaction between users and computers and the construction of interfaces that support this interaction," an interaction that occurs at an interface including both software and hardware. The field is supported by the ACM Special Interest Group on Computer-Human Interaction (SIGCHI), which describes itself as "the world's largest association of professionals who contribute towards the research and practice of human-computer interaction (HCI)." Its flagship venue is the ACM CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, described by SIGCHI as "the premier international conference of Human-Computer Interaction."

label: Computer Graphics
summary: Computer graphics is the subfield of computer science concerned with the generation, manipulation, and rendering of visual images and interactive content using computational systems. ACM SIGGRAPH describes itself as "an international community of researchers, artists, developers, filmmakers, scientists and business professionals with a shared interest in computer graphics and interactive techniques," with a mission "to nurture, champion and connect like-minded researchers and practitioners to catalyze innovation in computer graphics and interactive techniques." The organization offers "two of the premier conferences on computer graphics and interactive techniques in the world," SIGGRAPH and SIGGRAPH Asia, attended by tens of thousands of computer graphics professionals.

label: Cryptography
summary: Cryptography is the science of constructing and analyzing techniques for securing communications and data against adversarial access, encompassing both the design of encryption schemes and the analysis of their security. Britannica's entry on cryptology defines the field as "the science concerned with data communication and storage in secure and usually secret form" and distinguishes cryptography from cryptanalysis, "the science (and art) of recovering or forging cryptographically secured information without knowledge of the key." The Encyclopedia of Mathematics covers the introduction of public-key cryptography by Diffie and Hellman and the RSA system of Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman, which is based on the fact that it is almost impossible, by presently known factorization algorithms, to recover two large prime numbers from their product. The International Association for Cryptologic Research (IACR), whose purpose is to further research in cryptology, publishes the Journal of Cryptology, Transactions on Symmetric Cryptology, and Communications in Cryptology, and sponsors the Crypto, Eurocrypt, and Asiacrypt conferences.

label: Computer Security
summary: Computer security is defined by Britannica as "the protection of computer systems and information from harm, theft, and unauthorized use." Britannica identifies the principal threats it addresses as data theft, vandalism (including destruction by computer viruses), fraud such as unauthorized fund transfers, and invasion of privacy through illegal access to personal financial or medical data. Among its foundational methods are access control by "assigning an individual password to each person who has access to a system" with automatic logging of activity, isolation of sensitive data on devices "normally inaccessible through the computer system," and encryption so that data "can be deciphered only by holders of a singular encryption key." Britannica notes that the importance of computer security grew with the spread of modems in the late 1960s, personal computers in the 1980s, and the subsequent expansion of the Internet.

label: Theoretical Computer Science
summary: Theoretical computer science (TCS) is the branch of computer science concerned with the formal analysis of efficient computation and computational processes. The ACM Special Interest Group on Algorithms and Computation Theory (SIGACT) characterizes TCS as covering "algorithms, data structures, computational complexity, parallel and distributed computation, probabilistic computation, quantum computation, automata theory, information theory, cryptography, program semantics and verification, machine learning, computational biology, computational economics, computational geometry, and computational number theory and algebra," with work in the field distinguished by its emphasis on mathematical technique and rigor. SIGACT itself is described as an international organization that "fosters and promotes the discovery and dissemination of high quality research in theoretical computer science." Among the conferences SIGACT sponsors are STOC and ITCS, with in-cooperation venues including SODA and FOCS.

label: Formal Languages and Automata Theory
summary: Formal languages and automata theory is the branch of theoretical computer science that studies abstract machines and the classes of languages they recognize. The Encyclopedia of Mathematics describes a finite automaton as "a mathematical model of a system with a finite memory which processes discrete information," given formally as a system of an input alphabet, a set of states, and an output alphabet with transition and output functions, and calls it "the starting point of the modern theory of automata." The same source establishes the correspondence at the heart of the field: "events representable by a finite automaton are identical with so-called regular events," linking machine models to the formal languages they define.

label: Scientific Computing
summary: Scientific computing, also called computational science, sits at the interface of computer science and applied mathematics, developing the algorithms, mathematical models, and high-performance computing techniques used to simulate problems across the sciences and engineering. Britannica’s entry defines computational science as applying “computer simulation, scientific visualization, mathematical modeling, algorithms, data structures, networking, database design, symbolic computation, and high-performance computing to help advance the goals of various disciplines.” Its interdisciplinary character is reflected in its scholarly homes: the Journal of Scientific Computing describes itself as “an international interdisciplinary forum for the publication of papers on state-of-the-art developments in scientific computing and its applications in science and engineering,” while SIAM’s Computational Science and Engineering activity group fosters “collaboration and interaction among applied mathematicians, computer scientists, domain scientists and engineers” and promotes simulation “as a mode of scientific discovery on the same level as theory and experiment.”

label: Information Retrieval
summary: Information retrieval is the subfield of computer science and library and information science concerned with the representation, storage, and retrieval of information in response to queries. Britannica defines information retrieval as the "recovery of information, especially in a database stored in a computer," with methods that include keyword searching, navigation by hypertext links, and techniques incorporating natural language processing. ACM SIGIR, the Association for Computing Machinery's Special Interest Group on Information Retrieval, has since 1963 promoted "research, development and education in the area of search and other information access technologies"; its conference series dates to the 1971 International ACM SIGIR Conference on Information Storage and Retrieval, and the group publishes the SIGIR Forum.

label: Quantum Computing
summary: Quantum computing lies at the interface of computer science and the natural sciences, particularly physics, studying how the principles of quantum mechanics can be harnessed to perform computation. Britannica defines a quantum computer as a “device that employs properties described by quantum mechanics to enhance computations.” Its grounding in physics is visible in research classification: the Mathematics Subject Classification places “Quantum computation” (81P68) under its top-level quantum-theory class, the arXiv category taxonomy lists the quantum-physics archive quant-ph under the top-level “Physics” group, and Caltech’s Institute for Quantum Information and Matter is “a National Science Foundation Physics Frontiers Center” whose programs draw on “quantum information, atomic-molecular optical physics, and condensed matter physics.” Its computer-science dimension is equally explicit: the journal npj Quantum Information states that it “aims to develop and encourage the global exchange of ideas between physicists, computer scientists, material scientists, engineers, mathematicians, and other researchers who are active at the frontiers of these fields.”

label: Library and Information Science
summary: Library and information science (LIS) is the field concerned with how society stores, retrieves, analyzes, manages, archives, and disseminates information, bridging the professional practice of librarianship with the scientific study of information. Members of the Association for Information Science and Technology (ASIS&T) — drawn from librarianship, linguistics, engineering, law, medicine, and other fields — share, in the association's words, "a common interest in improving the ways society stores, retrieves, analyzes, manages, archives and disseminates information." The Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology (JASIST), a fully refereed scholarly and technical periodical, has been published continuously since 1950 and publishes research and development in a wide range of subjects in information science and technology. The iSchools organization — an alliance of university schools and departments offering doctoral programs in the field — describes the discipline's scope as relying strongly on the social and behavioural sciences, computing, and linguistics, with topics including human-computer interaction, information organisation and access, and bibliometrics.

label: Knowledge Organization
summary: Knowledge organization is, in the ISKO Encyclopedia of Knowledge Organization, "a field of research, teaching and practice, which is mostly affiliated with library and information science," concerned with "describing, representing, filing and organizing documents and document representations as well as subjects and concepts both by humans and by computer programs." The field distinguishes knowledge organization processes—"cataloging, subject analysis, indexing, tagging and classification"—from knowledge organization systems such as classification systems, subject-heading lists, thesauri, and ontologies. Its scholarly society is the International Society for Knowledge Organization (ISKO), founded in 1989, which publishes the journal Knowledge Organization, formerly titled International Classification and founded in 1974.

label: Digital Libraries
