summary: Digital libraries is the subfield of library and information science and computer science concerned with the creation, management, preservation, and access of digital collections of information resources. Britannica notes that the development of digital libraries (also known as virtual libraries) means people "do not have to go to a building for some kinds of information," though "users still need help to locate the information they want." The ACM/IEEE Joint Conference on Digital Libraries (JCDL) — "a major international forum focusing on digital libraries and associated technical, practical, and social issues" — combines the annual conferences formerly sponsored separately by ACM and IEEE-CS, and presents awards including the Vannevar Bush Best Paper Award to persons who have made outstanding contributions to the field.

label: Bibliometrics
summary: Bibliometrics is the application of statistical and quantitative methods to the study of the production, communication, and use of scientific and scholarly publications. The international journal Scientometrics describes its scope as "original research on all quantitative aspects of the production, communication, and use of scientific and technological information," welcoming both theoretical and empirical studies. The International Society for Scientometrics and Informetrics (ISSI) is an international association of scholars and professionals active in the interdisciplinary study of science, whose community focuses on quantitative approaches including informetrics, scientometrics, and webometrics.

label: Social Computing
summary: Social computing is the area of computer science that studies the design and use of computational systems and technologies in relation to social behavior, interaction, and organizations. The ACM Conference on Computer-Supported Cooperative Work and Social Computing (CSCW) is described as "the premier venue for research in the design and use of technologies that affect groups, organizations, communities, and networks," exploring "the technical, social, material, and theoretical challenges of designing technology to support collaborative work and life activities." Its 29th edition, CSCW 2026, is scheduled for Salt Lake City, Utah, in October 2026.

label: Visualization
summary: Visualization (in computing) is the study and practice of transforming data into visual representations to support tasks ranging from rapid observation to in-depth analysis. The IEEE VIS conference—the field's primary venue—defines visualization as "the study of the transformation of data to visual representations, which provide cost-effective means for supporting a variety of data intelligence tasks," and describes it as having expanded to encompass scientific visualization, information visualization, and visual analytics. IEEE VIS organizes research across areas including theoretical and empirical work, visualization systems and rendering, data transformations, and visual analytics for decision-making.

label: History of Computing
summary: History of computing is the scholarly study of the development of computing technology and its theoretical, institutional, and social contexts. Britannica records key milestones in that development, including the 1936 specification of the Turing machine by the British mathematician Alan Turing as a milestone in theoretical work on computability that began in the 1930s, the stored-program concept credited to the Hungarian-American mathematician John von Neumann, and the emergence of computer science "as an independent discipline in the early 1960s, although the electronic digital computer that is the object of its study was invented some two decades earlier." The Computer History Museum in Mountain View, California, which "collect[s] and care[s] for the artifacts and stories of the ongoing computing revolution," is among the institutions devoted to preserving this history.

label: Chemistry
summary: Chemistry is one of the natural sciences, concerned with the substances that make up matter and the changes they undergo. The Encyclopaedia Britannica describes it as "the science of the properties, composition, and structure of substances (defined as elements and compounds), the transformations they undergo, and the energy that is released or absorbed during these processes," noting that chemistry "is concerned with the properties of atoms and the laws governing their combinations." As a top-level field it serves as an umbrella over numerous specialized subfields, including analytical, inorganic, organic, and physical chemistry, as well as crystallography and electrochemistry, each addressing a distinct aspect of the composition, structure, reactivity, or measurement of chemical systems. Its central focus on atoms, molecules, and their transformations distinguishes it from neighboring natural-science fields while linking it closely to physics, the earth sciences, and the life sciences.

label: Astronomy
summary: Astronomy is the natural science devoted to celestial objects and the phenomena that occur beyond Earth's atmosphere. The Encyclopaedia Britannica characterizes it as the "science that encompasses the study of all extraterrestrial objects and phenomena," adding that "since the late 19th century, astronomy has expanded to include astrophysics, the application of physical and chemical knowledge to an understanding of the nature of celestial objects." As a top-level field within the natural sciences, it studies bodies such as stars, planets, galaxies, and the interstellar and intergalactic medium, as well as the structure and evolution of the universe as a whole. Modern astronomy draws heavily on physics and chemistry through astrophysics, and on observational techniques spanning the electromagnetic spectrum and beyond. It is conventionally treated as a discipline distinct from, though closely allied with, physics and the other physical sciences.

label: Earth Sciences
summary: The earth sciences form the top-level natural-science field concerned with the planet Earth as a physical system. The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines them as "the fields of study concerned with the solid Earth, its waters, and the air that envelops it," noting that "included are the geologic, hydrologic, and atmospheric sciences" and that "their broad aim is to understand Earth's present features and past evolution and to use this knowledge to benefit humankind." As an umbrella field, the earth sciences encompass a range of specialized disciplines—among them geology, which studies the solid Earth, alongside the sciences of the oceans, fresh waters, and atmosphere. The field investigates Earth's composition, structure, processes, and history across spatial and temporal scales, and it connects closely with the other natural sciences, including chemistry and physics, through the study of materials, energy, and planetary processes.

label: Environmental Science
summary: Environmental science is an interdisciplinary natural-science field that, in Encyclopaedia Britannica's words, is an "interdisciplinary academic field that draws on ecology, geology, meteorology, biology, chemistry, engineering, and physics to study environmental problems and human impacts on the environment." Nature Portfolio similarly defines it as "the multidisciplinary study of all aspects of the Earth's physical and biological environments," encompassing areas such as environmental chemistry, soil science, ecology, and climatology. The field is distinguished from environmental studies, which Britannica notes "emphasizes the human relationship with the environment and the social and political dimensions thereof." Classification systems place it among the natural sciences: the Universal Decimal Classification files "Environmental science. Conservation of natural resources. Threats to the environment and protection against them" within its main class 5, "MATHEMATICS. NATURAL SCIENCES." Together these sources frame environmental science as a bridging discipline that integrates multiple natural-science domains.

label: Condensed Matter Physics
summary: Condensed matter physics studies the properties of solid and liquid substances—materials whose constituent atoms remain in constant proximity. Encyclopaedia Britannica describes it as the "discipline that treats the thermal, elastic, electrical, magnetic, and optical properties of solid and liquid substances." The American Physical Society's Division of Condensed Matter Physics, which the society states was "Originally called the Division of Solid State Physics (DSSP)" before being "renamed the Division of Condensed Matter Physics to recognize that disciplines covered in the division included liquids (quantum fluids) as well as solids," characterizes the field as concentrating "on such topics as superconductivity, semi-conductors, magnetism, complex fluids, and thin films," with "A broad range of physical problems, both applied and basic" investigated. In the Physics Subject Headings (PhySH) scheme maintained by the American Physical Society it appears as the discipline "Condensed Matter, Materials & Applied Physics."

label: Atomic, Molecular and Optical Physics
summary: Atomic, molecular and optical (AMO) physics concerns the structure of atoms and simple molecules and their interactions with electrons and with light. The American Physical Society's Division of Atomic, Molecular and Optical Physics (DAMOP) describes its "central focus" as "fundamental research on atoms, simple molecules, electrons and light, and their interactions," noting that it works "through the development of methods for the control and manipulation of atoms, molecules, charged particles and light, through precision measurements and calculations of their properties, and through the invention of new ways to generate light with specific properties." The atomic component is treated by Encyclopaedia Britannica as "the scientific study of the structure of the atom, its energy states, and its interactions with other particles and with electric and magnetic fields." In the Physics Subject Headings (PhySH) scheme maintained by the American Physical Society the field appears as the discipline "Atomic, Molecular & Optical."

label: Optics
summary: Optics is the science of light: its origin, its propagation, and the changes it undergoes and produces. Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "science concerned with the genesis and propagation of light and with the changes that it undergoes and produces," and distinguishes its principal branches, stating that "Physical optics deals with the nature of light itself" while "Geometrical optics has to do with the principles that govern the image-forming properties of devices that make use of light." Optica, a scientific society in the field, describes itself as "the leading society in optics and photonics," pairing optics with photonics as its disciplinary domain. The field has a top-level entry (UDC 535 'Optics') in the Universal Decimal Classification scheme.

label: Nuclear Physics
summary: Nuclear physics studies the atomic nucleus, the properties of nuclei and nuclear matter, and the interactions of their constituents. The American Physical Society's Division of Nuclear Physics describes itself as "comprised of scientists and educators who study fundamental problems related to the nature of matter," explaining that "Nuclear scientists probe the properties of nuclei and nuclear matter and the interactions of their ultimate constituents — quarks and gluons." In the Physics Subject Headings (PhySH) scheme maintained by the American Physical Society the field appears as the discipline "Nuclear Physics."

label: Particle Physics
summary: Particle physics studies the fundamental subatomic particles and the forces through which they interact. Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "Study of the fundamental subatomic particles, including both matter (and antimatter) and the carrier particles of the fundamental interactions as described by quantum field theory," adding that it "is concerned with structure and forces at this level of existence and below." The American Physical Society's Division of Particles and Fields gives its objective as "the study of fundamental particles and fields, their structure, their interactions and interrelationships, the design and development of high energy accelerators, and the design and development of instrumentation techniques for high energy physics." In the Physics Subject Headings (PhySH) scheme maintained by the American Physical Society it appears as the discipline "Particles & Fields."

label: Plasma Physics
summary: Plasma physics studies plasmas—ionized media containing roughly equal numbers of positively and negatively charged particles. Encyclopaedia Britannica describes plasma as "an electrically conducting medium in which there are roughly equal numbers of positively and negatively charged particles, produced when the atoms in a gas become ionized," and notes it "is sometimes referred to as the fourth state of matter, distinct from the solid, liquid, and gaseous states." The American Physical Society's Division of Plasma Physics states that its objective is "the advancement and dissemination of the knowledge, understanding, and applications of plasmas—assemblages of charged particles of natural and laboratory origin," spanning "the study of the fundamental interactions of particles and light in plasmas, the study of astrophysical plasmas from planetary cores to stars, new theoretical and computational techniques to describe plasmas, and the practical application of plasmas." In the Physics Subject Headings (PhySH) scheme maintained by the American Physical Society it appears as the discipline "Plasma Physics."

label: Fluid Dynamics
summary: Fluid dynamics studies the motion of fluids—liquids and gases—and their response to forces. Encyclopaedia Britannica defines the broader field of fluid mechanics as the "science concerned with the response of fluids to forces exerted upon them," identifying it as "a branch of classical physics." The American Physical Society's Division of Fluid Dynamics states that it "exists for the advancement and diffusion of knowledge of the physics of fluids with special emphasis on the dynamical theories of the liquid, plastic and gaseous states of matter under all conditions of temperature and pressure." In the Physics Subject Headings (PhySH) scheme maintained by the American Physical Society it appears as the discipline "Fluid Dynamics."

label: Statistical Physics and Thermodynamics
summary: Statistical physics applies statistical methods to systems of many constituents in order to derive their macroscopic properties from the behavior of their microscopic parts. Encyclopaedia Britannica defines statistical mechanics—a core component—as the "branch of physics that combines the principles and procedures of statistics with the laws of both classical and quantum mechanics, particularly with respect to the field of thermodynamics," noting that "It aims to predict and explain the measurable properties of macroscopic systems" from their microscopic constituents. The related discipline of thermodynamics is defined by Britannica as the "science of the relationship between heat, work, temperature, and energy." In the Physics Subject Headings (PhySH) scheme maintained by the American Physical Society the field appears as the discipline "Statistical Physics & Thermodynamics."

label: Acoustics
summary: Acoustics is the science of sound—its production, control, transmission, reception, and effects. Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "science concerned with the production, control, transmission, reception, and effects of sound," noting that it began "with its origins in the study of mechanical vibrations and the radiation of these vibrations through mechanical waves." Within the Universal Decimal Classification the field is grouped under UDC 534 'Vibrations. Waves. Acoustics,' reflecting its grounding in vibration and wave phenomena.

label: Biophysics
summary: Biophysics is a discipline at the interface of the physical and life sciences. Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as a "discipline concerned with the application of the principles and methods of physics and the other physical sciences to the solution of biological problems," noting that biophysics and the closely related molecular biology "now are firmly established as cornerstones of modern biology." The Biophysical Society, the field's principal professional society, states its mission as "To lead an innovative global community working at the interface of the physical and life sciences, across all levels of complexity," reflecting a community that spans both parent domains rather than residing in one alone. Classification practice mirrors this dual character: the Universal Decimal Classification files biophysics under its life-sciences captions, listing "Material bases of life. Biochemistry. Molecular biology. Biophysics" within "Biological sciences in general," while physics communities study the same subject matter under headings such as the physics of living systems.

label: Nonlinear Dynamics
summary: Nonlinear dynamics studies systems whose governing equations are nonlinear, giving rise to phenomena such as chaos, pattern formation, and turbulence. The American Physical Society's Division on Statistical and Nonlinear Physics (originally a Topical Group) describes its community as "scientists working on statistical physics and nonlinear dynamics problems, such as phase transitions and critical phenomena, turbulence, pattern formation, avalanches, and chaotic dynamics." Chaotic behavior, a central concern of the field, is characterized by Encyclopaedia Britannica as "the study of apparently random or unpredictable behavior in systems governed by deterministic laws." In the Physics Subject Headings (PhySH) scheme maintained by the American Physical Society the field appears as the discipline "Nonlinear Dynamics."

label: Accelerator Physics
summary: Accelerator physics concerns the production, behavior, and use of beams of charged particles and the instruments that generate them. The American Physical Society's Division of Physics of Beams gives its objective as "the advancement and diffusion of knowledge regarding the nature and behavior of beams and the instruments for their production and use." The principal instruments of the field, particle accelerators, are described by Encyclopaedia Britannica as "any device that produces a beam of fast-moving, electrically charged atomic or subatomic particles," used "in fundamental research on the structure of nuclei, the nature of nuclear forces, and the properties of nuclei not found in nature." In the Physics Subject Headings (PhySH) scheme maintained by the American Physical Society the field appears as the discipline "Accelerators & Beams."

label: Soft Matter Physics
summary: Soft matter physics studies materials that are readily deformed by thermal fluctuations or modest external stresses, including colloids, polymers, gels, foams, and biological and granular matter. The American Physical Society's Division of Soft Matter describes soft matter as "a broad class of physical states ranging from colloids and micelles to biological and granular matter that are easily deformed by external stresses," adding that "The common feature of these materials is that the predominant physical behaviors occur at energy scales comparable with thermal energy." Its stated mission is to "advance knowledge and build community among the interdisciplinary group of scientists, mathematicians, and engineers working on soft matter physics." In the Physics Subject Headings (PhySH) scheme maintained by the American Physical Society it appears within the discipline "Polymers & Soft Matter."

label: Analytical Chemistry
summary: Analytical chemistry is the subfield of chemistry concerned with determining the composition of matter and the identity, quantity, and structure of its components. The Encyclopaedia Britannica, treating the subject under chemical analysis, describes it as the "determination of the physical properties or chemical composition of samples of matter," noting that "a large body of systematic procedures intended for these purposes has been continuously evolving in close association with the development of other branches of the physical sciences." The disciplinary community frames the field around measurement science: the journal Analytical and Bioanalytical Chemistry states that its scope covers "fundamental and applied topics of analytical and bioanalytical measurement science" and "ranges from novel measurement platforms and their characterization to multidisciplinary approaches." The subfield develops and applies methods of qualitative and quantitative analysis, instrumentation, and separation and detection techniques used throughout the natural sciences.

label: Inorganic Chemistry
summary: Inorganic chemistry is the subfield of chemistry concerned with the elements and compounds that fall outside the domain of carbon-based organic chemistry. The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "field of science concerned with the composition, properties, and structure of chemical elements and compounds that contain little or no carbon," and explicitly contrasts it with organic chemistry: "It is distinguished from organic chemistry, which studies compounds that contain carbon atoms." The subfield encompasses the chemistry of metals and minerals, coordination compounds, main-group and transition-element species, and solid-state and organometallic systems, addressing their synthesis, bonding, structure, and reactivity. Within the broader field of chemistry it occupies a recognized major subdivision alongside the organic, physical, and analytical subfields, and it underpins areas such as materials science, catalysis, and the study of inorganic substances throughout the natural sciences.

label: Organic Chemistry
summary: Organic chemistry is the subfield of chemistry devoted to compounds of carbon. The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "field of science concerned with the composition, properties, and structure of chemical elements and compounds that contain carbon atoms," and explains the field's breadth by noting that "carbon is unique in the variety and extent of structures that can result from the three-dimensional connections of its atoms." The subfield studies the structure, properties, synthesis, and reactions of carbon-containing molecules, ranging from small hydrocarbons to large and structurally elaborate compounds. Within the broader field of chemistry it constitutes a recognized major subdivision, distinguished from inorganic chemistry by its focus on carbon, and it connects closely with the life sciences and with applied areas that rely on the synthesis and transformation of carbon compounds.

label: Physical Chemistry
summary: Physical chemistry is the subfield of chemistry that applies the principles of physics to chemical systems. The Encyclopaedia Britannica describes it as the "branch of chemistry concerned with interactions and transformations of materials," explaining that, "unlike other branches, it deals with the principles of physics underlying all chemical interactions, seeking to measure, correlate, and explain the quantitative aspects of reactions." The subfield encompasses areas such as thermodynamics, chemical kinetics, quantum chemistry, spectroscopy, electrochemistry, and statistical mechanics, providing the quantitative and theoretical foundations used across the rest of chemistry. Within the broader field it forms a recognized major subdivision alongside the analytical, inorganic, and organic subfields, and it serves as a bridge between chemistry and physics in the study of how matter behaves at the molecular and bulk levels.

label: Biochemistry
summary: Biochemistry is a discipline at the interface of chemistry and the life sciences. Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as "the study of the chemical substances and processes that occur in plants, animals, and microorganisms and of the changes they undergo during development and life." Its dual character is visible in classification systems: the Library of Congress Classification files biochemistry under the hierarchy "Science--Chemistry--Organic chemistry--Biochemistry," while Britannica's own subject breadcrumb places the article under Science > Biology > Branches of Biology, and the Universal Decimal Classification lists "Material bases of life. Biochemistry. Molecular biology. Biophysics" under "Biological sciences in general." The American Society for Biochemistry and Molecular Biology describes its community as "molecular life scientists" and frames its mission as advancing understanding of "the molecular nature of life processes," reflecting a field that draws co-equally on chemical methods and biological subject matter.

label: Crystallography
summary: Crystallography is the subfield concerned with the internal arrangement of matter in crystalline solids. The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "branch of science that deals with discerning the arrangement and bonding of atoms in crystalline solids and with the geometric structure of crystal lattices," and notes that "classically, the optical properties of crystals were of value in mineralogy and chemistry for the identification of substances." The subfield studies how atoms, ions, and molecules are ordered in periodic structures and the symmetry and geometry of crystal lattices, and it develops and applies experimental methods—diffraction techniques in particular—for determining such structures. Historically allied with mineralogy and chemistry, crystallography provides structural information used widely across the natural sciences, including in the study of minerals, inorganic and organic compounds, and biological macromolecules.

label: Electrochemistry
summary: Electrochemistry is the subfield of chemistry that studies the relationship between electricity and chemical change. The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "branch of chemistry concerned with the relation between electricity and chemical change," noting that "many spontaneously occurring chemical reactions liberate electrical energy, and some of these reactions are used in batteries and fuel cells to produce electric power," while conversely electric energy can be used to drive chemical reactions. The subfield encompasses the study of oxidation–reduction processes, electrodes and electrolytes, electrolysis, and the behavior of ions and charge transfer at interfaces. It underlies technologies such as batteries, fuel cells, electroplating, and corrosion science, and is conventionally treated as closely associated with physical chemistry within the broader field of chemistry.

label: Astrophysics
summary: Astrophysics is the branch of astronomy that studies the physical properties, composition, and structure of celestial objects and of the universe as a whole, applying the laws of physics to understand cosmic phenomena. The Encyclopaedia Britannica characterizes it as the "branch of astronomy concerned primarily with the properties and structure of cosmic objects, including the universe as a whole." Its identity as a distinct division within astronomy is reflected in standard bibliographic classification: the Library of Congress Classification assigns the range QB460-QB466 to "Astrophysics (General)" within the astronomy subclass QB. The field connects observational astronomy with theoretical physics, treating objects such as stars, galaxies, and interstellar matter as physical systems whose behavior can be modeled through the same principles that govern matter and energy on Earth.

label: Cosmology
summary: Cosmology is the study of the physical universe taken as a unified whole, including its large-scale structure, origin, and evolution. The Encyclopaedia Britannica describes it as the "field of study that brings together the natural sciences, particularly astronomy and physics, in a joint effort to understand the physical universe as a unified whole," noting that at the largest scales a distinctive feature emerges in the form of the cosmological expansion. As a recognized division of astronomical study, it occupies its own place in standard library classification: the Library of Congress Classification assigns the range QB980-QB991 the label "Cosmogony. Cosmology" within the astronomy subclass QB. The discipline draws jointly on astronomy and physics to describe phenomena that have no counterpart at smaller, local scales.

label: Planetary Science
summary: Planetary science is the study of planets and other bodies of the solar system, addressing their origin, evolution, structure, and physical and chemical characteristics. NASA's planetary science program "explores the objects in our solar system to better understand its history and the distribution of life within." The field's standing as a distinct area within astronomy is reflected in standard library classification, where the Library of Congress Classification assigns the range QB600-QB701 to "Planets. Planetology" within the astronomy subclass QB. Its scholarly community is institutionalized: the Division for Planetary Sciences (DPS), described in its own materials as "the world's largest professional society of planetary scientists," is a division of the American Astronomical Society.

label: Geology
summary: Geology is the study of the solid Earth — its materials, structure, processes, and history. The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as comprising "the fields of study concerned with the solid Earth," noting that geology "also explores geologic history, which provides a conceptual framework and overview of Earth's evolution." Its scope spans the description of Earth materials, the processes that shape the planet, and the reconstruction of past conditions from the rock record. As a major division of the sciences, geology occupies the entire QE subclass of the Library of Congress Classification.

label: Geophysics
summary: Geophysics applies the principles and methods of physics to the study of the Earth. The Encyclopaedia Britannica describes it as a "major branch of the Earth sciences that applies the principles and methods of physics to the study of the Earth," dealing with a wide range of geologic phenomena. Its dual character as both an Earth science and a physics-based discipline is mirrored in standard bibliographic classification: the Library of Congress Classification places "Geophysics. Cosmic physics" at QC801-QC809, within the physics subclass QC rather than the geology subclass QE. The field uses physical observations — of gravity, magnetism, seismic wave propagation, heat, and related quantities — to infer the composition, structure, and dynamics of the Earth's interior and surface.

label: Geochemistry
summary: Geochemistry is the scientific study of the chemistry of the Earth, focusing on the relative abundance, distribution, and movement of the chemical elements and their isotopes within the planet. The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "scientific discipline that deals with the relative abundance, distribution, and migration of the Earth's chemical elements and their isotopes." The field examines how elements are partitioned among the Earth's materials and reservoirs and how they migrate through geologic processes over time. Geochemistry sits at the interface of the geological and chemical sciences, drawing on chemical analysis and theory to characterize the composition and evolution of rocks, minerals, waters, and other Earth materials.

label: Mineralogy
summary: Mineralogy is the scientific study of minerals in all their aspects. The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "scientific discipline that is concerned with all aspects of minerals, including their physical properties, chemical composition, internal crystal structure, and occurrence and distribution in nature and their origins in terms of the physicochemical conditions of formation." The field characterizes naturally occurring crystalline substances by their composition, structure, and properties, and investigates the conditions under which they form. Its identity as an established subject is reflected in standard library classification, where the Library of Congress Classification assigns the range QE351-QE399.2 the label "Mineralogy" within the geology subclass QE.

label: Petrology
summary: Petrology is the branch of geology concerned with rocks — their composition, texture, structure, occurrence, and origin. The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "scientific study of rocks that deals with their composition, texture, and structure; their occurrence and distribution; and their origin in relation to physicochemical conditions and geologic processes," and notes that it addresses all three major rock types: igneous, metamorphic, and sedimentary. The field interprets rocks as records of the physical and chemical conditions under which they formed. Its standing as an established subject is reflected in standard library classification, where the Library of Congress Classification assigns the range QE420-QE499 the label "Petrology" within the geology subclass QE.

label: Paleontology
summary: Paleontology is the scientific study of past life as preserved in the fossil record. The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "scientific study of life of the geologic past that involves the analysis of plant and animal fossils, including those of microscopic size, preserved in rocks," and notes that it "has played a key role in reconstructing Earth's history and has provided much evidence to support the theory of evolution." The discipline reconstructs the history of life and ancient environments from fossils ranging from microscopic remains to large organisms. Its identity as an established subject is reflected in standard library classification, where the Library of Congress Classification assigns the range QE701-QE760 the label "Paleontology" within the geology subclass QE.

label: Seismology
summary: Seismology is the study of earthquakes and of the propagation of seismic waves through the Earth. The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "scientific discipline that is concerned with the study of earthquakes and of the propagation of seismic waves within the Earth," describing it as a branch of geophysics that has "provided much information about the composition and state of the planet's interior." The field uses recordings of seismic waves both to characterize earthquake sources and to probe the Earth's internal structure. Its scholarly community is institutionalized in bodies such as the Seismological Society of America, which presents its mission in terms of advancing "the science of seismology."

label: Volcanology
summary: Volcanology is the branch of the geologic sciences concerned with volcanoes and volcanic phenomena. The Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "discipline of the geologic sciences that is concerned with all aspects of volcanic phenomena," addressing "the formation, distribution, and classification of volcanoes as well as with their structure and the kinds of materials ejected during an eruption." The field studies how volcanoes form and are distributed, the products of eruptions, and the processes that drive volcanic activity. In the Library of Congress Classification, volcanoes are treated alongside earthquakes in the range QE521-QE545, labeled "Volcanoes and earthquakes," within the geology subclass QE.

label: Oceanography
summary: Oceanography is an earth science concerned with the world's oceans and seas. Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "scientific discipline concerned with all aspects of the world's oceans and seas, including their physical and chemical properties, their origin and geologic framework, and the life forms that inhabit the marine environment." Britannica's subject breadcrumb places the article under Science > Earth Science, Geologic Time & Fossils > Earth Sciences. Classification systems likewise group it with the earth sciences: the Universal Decimal Classification lists "Physical oceanography. Submarine topography. Ocean floor" among the captions of its earth-sciences division. Oceanography shares adjacency with physical geography, but its disciplinary home, as reflected in reference and classification sources, is the earth sciences.

label: Atmospheric Science
summary: Atmospheric science is the study of the structure, composition, and dynamics of Earth's atmosphere. The Encyclopaedia Britannica describes it as an "interdisciplinary field of study that combines the components of physics and chemistry that focus on the structure and dynamics of Earth's atmosphere." As an umbrella discipline, it encompasses several traditional areas; Britannica notes that "the atmospheric sciences are traditionally divided into three topical areas—meteorology (the study and forecasting of weather), climatology (the study of long-term atmospheric patterns and their influences), and aeronomy (the study of the physics and chemistry of the upper atmosphere)." The field draws on mathematical and computational tools to describe physical and chemical processes spanning timescales from hourly weather changes to long-term climate, treating meteorology and climatology as branches within its scope rather than as separate disciplines.

label: Hydrology
summary: Hydrology is an earth science concerned with the waters of the Earth. Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "scientific discipline concerned with the waters of the Earth, including their occurrence, distribution, and circulation via the hydrologic cycle and interactions with living things," adding that it "also deals with the chemical and physical properties of water in all its phases." Britannica's subject breadcrumb places the article under Science > Earth Science, Geologic Time & Fossils > Earth Sciences. The Universal Decimal Classification similarly files "Hydrosphere. Water in general. Hydrology" within its division "Earth Sciences. Geological sciences." Hydrology shares adjacency with physical geography, but classification and reference sources frame its disciplinary home as the earth sciences.

label: Geomorphology
summary: Geomorphology is an earth science concerned with the Earth's surface forms. Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "scientific discipline concerned with the description and classification of the Earth's topographic features" and directs readers, for fuller treatment, to its article on geology, indicating its close alignment with the geological sciences. The Universal Decimal Classification files it under the caption "Geomorphology. Study of the Earth's physical forms" within its earth-sciences division. Geomorphology shares adjacency with physical geography, but its disciplinary home, as reflected in reference and classification sources, is the earth sciences.

label: Geodesy
summary: Geodesy is the science of measuring the Earth's geometry and physical fields, occupying a dual position between astronomy and the earth sciences. The International Association of Geodesy describes its primary aim as to "determine the size, shape, gravity field and rotation of the Earth" as a function of space and time, monitoring the Earth system and measuring global change. Its classical heritage is preserved in library systems: the Library of Congress Classification files geodesy under "Science--Astronomy--Geodesy," and the Universal Decimal Classification places "Geodesy. Surveying. Photogrammetry. Remote sensing. Cartography" inside its class "Astronomy. Astrophysics. Space research. Geodesy." Its modern community framing, however, is geoscientific: the International Association of Geodesy is "one of the constituent associations of the International Union of Geodesy and Geophysics (IUGG)," situating contemporary geodesy among the geophysical and earth sciences.

label: Quantum Information Science
summary: Quantum information science is an emerging field at the intersection of quantum physics and information theory. NIST describes it as a field that "marries two of the 20th century's most important scientific developments: quantum physics and information theory," and characterizes it as "using the smallest bits of matter and energy — electrons inside an atom, tiny circuits, massless particles of light — to store, carry and process information." The field is broader than quantum computing alone: NIST notes that while "scientists around the world are developing quantum computers," "other focus areas of quantum information science include quantum sensors for ultra-high-precision measurements and quantum networks that could link devices across cities, nations and ultimately the globe." The Physics Subject Headings (PhySH) taxonomy lists "Quantum Information, Science & Technology" as a discipline-level research area, spanning quantum computation, communication, and sensing.

label: Economics
summary: Economics is the social science concerned with the production, distribution, and consumption of goods and services. The American Economic Association, a scholarly society in the field, describes economics on its student resources as "a broad discipline that helps us understand historical trends, interpret today's headlines, and make predictions about the coming years," noting that its study "ranges from the very small to the very large"—from microeconomics, "the study of individual decisions," to macroeconomics, "the study of the economy as a whole." The Association describes itself as "a nonprofit, nonpartisan, scholarly association with more than 17,000 members from academia, government, and business who are committed to the advancement of economics and its enduring contributions to society." In the Library of Congress Classification, economic theory falls within class HB, whose authority record bears the caption "Economic theory. Demography."

label: Sociology
summary: Sociology is the social science that studies human society and social behavior. The American Sociological Association, on its "What Is Sociology?" resource, defines it as "the study of social life, social change, and the social causes and consequences of human behavior," explaining that "Sociologists investigate the structure of groups, organizations, and societies and how people interact within these contexts," so that "the subject matter of sociology ranges from the intimate family to global communities." The Association describes itself as having been "founded in 1905" and as "the national professional membership association for sociologists and others who are interested in sociology," with a mission to "advance sociology as a science and profession, and promote the contributions and use of sociology to society." In the Library of Congress Classification the discipline occupies class HM, whose authority record carries the caption "Sociology."

label: Political Science
summary: Political science is the social science concerned with the study of government, politics, and power. Encyclopaedia Britannica describes it as "the systematic study of governance by the application of empirical and generally scientific methods of analysis," adding that "As traditionally defined and studied, political science examines the state and its organs and institutions." The American Political Science Association, founded in 1903, describes itself as bringing "together political scientists from all fields of inquiry, regions, and occupational endeavors within and outside academe to deepen our understanding of politics, democracy, and citizenship throughout the world." In the Library of Congress Classification the discipline's general works fall within class JA, whose authority record carries the caption "Political science (General)."

label: Education
summary: As an academic field, education is the scholarly discipline that studies teaching, learning, and the conditions under which they occur. Encyclopaedia Britannica describes education as "a discipline that is concerned with methods of teaching and learning in schools or school-like environments as opposed to various nonformal and informal means of socialization." The American Educational Research Association, a research society founded in 1916, describes itself as "a national research society" that "strives to advance knowledge about education, to encourage scholarly inquiry related to education, and to promote the use of research to improve education and serve the public good," and as "concerned with improving the educational process by encouraging scholarly inquiry related to education and evaluation." In the Library of Congress Classification, general works on education fall within class L, whose authority record carries the caption "Education (General)," with the theory and practice of education classed in LB.

label: Law
summary: As an academic discipline, law is the field of scholarship concerned with legal rules, institutions, and reasoning. Encyclopaedia Britannica describes law as "the discipline and profession concerned with the customs, practices, and rules of conduct of a community that are recognized as binding by the community," noting that "Enforcement of the body of rules is through a controlling authority." The Association of American Law Schools, which describes itself as "a 501(c)(3) nonprofit association" of member law schools, states that it was "Founded in 1900" and that its mission "is to improve and advance legal education," pursued "by promoting the core values of excellence in teaching and scholarship, academic freedom, and diversity of viewpoints." In the Library of Congress Classification the discipline occupies class K, whose general authority record carries the caption "Law in general. Comparative and uniform law. Jurisprudence."

label: Anthropology
summary: Anthropology is the social science that studies human beings, their societies, and their development. The American Anthropological Association, on its "What Is Anthropology?" resource, describes anthropology as "the study of what makes us human," explaining that to grasp "the full sweep and complexity of cultures across all of human history, anthropology draws and builds upon knowledge from the social and biological sciences as well as the humanities and physical sciences." The Association notes that "In the community of anthropologists in the United States, these four fields—human biology, archaeology, cultural anthropology, and linguistics—are understood to be the pillars on which the whole discipline rests," while observing that any individual anthropologist "will probably specialize in one or two of these areas but have general familiarity with them all." In the Library of Congress Classification the discipline occupies class GN, whose authority record carries the caption "Anthropology."

label: Econometrics
summary: Econometrics applies statistical and mathematical methods to the analysis of economic relationships, using data to estimate and test economic models. The learned society of the field, the Econometric Society, describes itself as "an international society for the advancement of economic theory in its relation to statistics and mathematics," and publishes the journals Econometrica, Quantitative Economics, and Theoretical Economics. In the American Economic Association's Journal of Economic Literature (JEL) classification, econometrics falls within category C, "Mathematical and Quantitative Methods," which includes the subcategory C5, "Econometric Modeling." Within the Library of Congress Classification the discipline is named in the schedule path "Mathematical economics. Quantitative methods--Econometrics" (class HB139). The Universal Decimal Classification places the closely related area of "Mathematical economics" at UDC 330.4.

label: Labor Economics
summary: Labour economics (also labor economics) studies the workforce and the markets through which labour is supplied and hired. Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "study of the labour force as an element in the process of production," explaining that "The labour force comprises all those who work for gain, whether as employees, employers, or as self-employed, and it includes the unemployed who are seeking work," and that the field "involves the study of the factors affecting the efficiency of these workers, their deployment between different industries and occupations, and the determination of their pay." In the American Economic Association's JEL classification the field falls within category J, "Labor and Demographic Economics." The Universal Decimal Classification groups it under UDC 331, "Labour. Employment. Work. Labour economics. Organization of labour."

label: Economic History
summary: Economic history examines economic systems and economic life as they have developed over time. Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "branch of historiography concerned with the history and development of economic systems and, more broadly, with the investigation of economic aspects of historical societies," noting that "The studies of history and economics were once closely related" and that political economists such as Adam Smith, Thomas Malthus, and Karl Marx "incorporated historical data into their analyses." The field is served by scholarly bodies including the Economic History Association, whose site (EH.net) hosts its annual meeting and publications. In the American Economic Association's JEL classification economic history forms its own top-level category, N, "Economic History."

label: Public Finance
summary: Public finance studies the revenue, expenditure, and debt operations of government and their effects on the economy. The Universal Decimal Classification gives the field a dedicated place at UDC 336.1, "Public sector finance. Government finance in general," nested within UDC 336, "Finance," alongside UDC 336.2, "Public revenue," and UDC 336.5, "Public expenditure. State expenditure." In the American Economic Association's Journal of Economic Literature classification the corresponding category is H, "Public Economics," which encompasses the subcategory H2, "Taxation, Subsidies, and Revenue." The field is served internationally by scholarly bodies such as the International Institute of Public Finance.

label: International Economics
summary: International economics studies economic transactions and relationships among nations, centring on international trade and international finance. Encyclopaedia Britannica defines international trade, the field's core subject, as "economic transactions that are made between countries," among which "are consumer goods, such as television sets and clothing; capital goods, such as machinery; and raw materials and food," with such transactions "facilitated by international financial payments." In the American Economic Association's JEL classification the field forms top-level category F, "International Economics," whose subcategory F1 covers "Trade." The Universal Decimal Classification groups the area under UDC 339, "Trade. Commerce. International economic relations. World economy," with UDC 339.5 covering "Foreign trade. External trade. International trade" and UDC 339.7 covering "International finance."

label: Financial Economics
summary: Financial economics studies the allocation of resources under uncertainty over time, including asset pricing, the behaviour of financial markets, and the financing decisions of firms and investors. In the American Economic Association's Journal of Economic Literature classification the field forms top-level category G, "Financial Economics," whose subcategory G1 covers "General Financial Markets" and which sits alongside the neighbouring economics categories in the same scheme. The Universal Decimal Classification places the area at UDC 336.7, "Money. Monetary system. Banking. Stock exchanges," within the broader UDC 336, "Finance," the same parent class under which public-sector finance and public revenue are also grouped. Scholarly societies in the field include the American Finance Association, publisher of The Journal of Finance.

label: Criminology
summary: Criminology is the multidisciplinary study of crime and of society's responses to it. The American Society of Criminology describes itself as "an international organization whose members pursue scholarly, scientific, and professional knowledge concerning the measurement, etiology, consequences, prevention, control, and treatment of crime and delinquency," and frames its work as occurring "in a multidisciplinary setting," publishing the journal Criminology: An Interdisciplinary Journal. The field sits at the intersection of several disciplines: in the Universal Decimal Classification it is placed at 343.9 "Criminology. Criminal sciences. Criminalistics" within the criminal-law class 343, where its scope is noted to include "Criminal sociology" and "Forensic psychology," reflecting its connections to law, sociology, and psychology alike.

label: Demography
summary: Demography is the scientific study of human populations. Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as the "statistical study of human populations, especially with reference to size and density, distribution, and vital statistics (births, marriages, deaths, etc.)." The International Union for the Scientific Study of Population (IUSSP) likewise describes demography as "the scientific study of human populations primarily with respect to their size, their structure and their development," stating that its own mission "is to promote the scientific study of population, encourage exchange between researchers around the globe, and stimulate interest in population issues." In the Universal Decimal Classification the field has a dedicated top-level place at UDC 314, "Demography. Population studies."

label: Social Work and Welfare
summary: Social work is both an academic discipline and a profession concerned with human well-being and social welfare. The Global Definition of the Social Work Profession, approved by the International Federation of Social Workers (IFSW) and the International Association of Schools of Social Work in July 2014, states: "Social work is a practice-based profession and an academic discipline that promotes social change and development, social cohesion, and the empowerment and liberation of people." The U.S. National Association of Social Workers characterizes it in practice terms, noting that "Social workers assist people by helping them cope with issues in their everyday lives, deal with their relationships, and solve personal and family problems." In the Universal Decimal Classification the area is grouped under class 36, "Safeguarding the mental and material necessities of life," which includes social work and the welfare subdivision 364 "Social welfare."

label: Gender Studies
summary: Gender studies is an interdisciplinary field examining gender, sex roles, and their social and cultural dimensions. It is recognized as a distinct area within the social sciences in the Universal Decimal Classification, which assigns it class 305 "Gender studies" directly under "3 SOCIAL SCIENCES," with the scope note "Including: Sex role. Gender. Persons from an interdisciplinary viewpoint," and lists "305-055.1 Men's studies" and "305-055.2 Women's studies" among its subdivisions. The UDC's explicit "interdisciplinary viewpoint" framing reflects the field's character, drawing together questions about gender that cut across multiple disciplines rather than belonging to any single one.

label: Social Stratification
summary: Social stratification is the study of structured inequalities between groups in society and of movement among social positions. It is a core area of sociology: in the Universal Decimal Classification, sociology occupies class 316 "Sociology," within which 316.3 is captioned "Social structure. Society as a social system." The field's principal international scholarly body is the Research Committee on Social Stratification and Mobility (RC28) of the International Sociological Association, whose page notes that "Research in Social Stratification and Mobility is the official journal of the ISA RC28." The committee's sustained focus on stratification and mobility situates the subfield within sociology's broader analysis of social structure.

label: International Relations
summary: International relations is the study of relations among states and other actors in world politics. Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as "the study of the relations of states with each other and with international organizations and certain subnational entities (e.g., bureaucracies, political parties, and interest groups)," adding that "It is related to a number of other academic disciplines, including political science, geography, history, economics, law, sociology, psychology, and philosophy." As a recognized branch of political science, it has dedicated scholarly infrastructure: the International Studies Association describes itself as "one of the oldest interdisciplinary associations dedicated to understanding international, transnational and global affairs," "Founded in 1959." In the Universal Decimal Classification the field appears at 327, "International relations. World, global politics. International affairs. Foreign policy."

label: Public Administration
summary: Public administration is the field concerned with the organization, management, and delivery of government and public services. Its principal accrediting and membership body is the Network of Schools of Public Policy, Affairs, and Administration (NASPAA), which describes itself as "the recognized global accreditor of master's degree programs in these fields" and as "a nonprofit 501(c)(3) membership association with over 300 institutional member schools at U.S. and non-U.S. universities that award degrees in public administration, public policy, public affairs, non profit and related fields." NASPAA states that its "twofold mission is to ensure excellence in education and training for public service and to promote the ideal of public service." In the Universal Decimal Classification, public administration is placed directly under the social sciences as "35 Public administration. Government. Military affairs."

label: Comparative Politics
summary: Comparative politics is a branch of political science that studies and compares political systems, institutions, and political behaviour across countries. The Library of Congress Classification files comparative government within class JF, "Political institutions and public administration (General)" (JF20-JF2112), whose schedule carries the caption "General. Comparative government." In the Universal Decimal Classification the subject falls within the politics class, captioned "32 Politics" and placed under "3 SOCIAL SCIENCES," alongside subdivisions such as "321 Forms of political organization. States as political powers." Through these gate classifications the comparative study of states, regimes, constitutions, and forms of political organization is situated within the discipline of political science.

label: Curriculum and Instruction
summary: Curriculum and instruction is the field of education research concerned with what is taught and how it is taught: the design, organization, and content of curricula and the didactic methods by which they are delivered. Within the American Educational Research Association the field is institutionalized as Division B, "Curriculum Studies," and Division C, "Learning & Instruction," two of the association's standing research divisions. In the Universal Decimal Classification its instructional dimension is grouped under UDC 37.02, captioned "General questions of didactics and method," within the education class (UDC 37). The field examines curriculum aims, subject matter, instructional design, and methods of teaching across the elementary, secondary, and tertiary levels.

label: Educational Policy
summary: Educational policy is the field of education research that studies the formation, content, and effects of the policies and political processes governing education systems. Within the American Educational Research Association it is institutionalized as Division L, "Educational Policy & Politics," one of the association's standing research divisions. In the Universal Decimal Classification the policy and theory of education are grouped under UDC 37.01, captioned "Fundamentals of education. Theory, policy, etc.," within the education class (UDC 37). The field analyzes how educational policy is made and implemented and how it shapes practice across levels of schooling.

label: Higher Education
summary: Higher education, as a field of study, is the scholarly inquiry into postsecondary (tertiary) education: its institutions, organization, policy, and outcomes. The Association for the Study of Higher Education (ASHE) describes itself as "a vibrant scholarly community ... dedicated to advancing the study of higher education," with the stated purpose "To foster scholarly inquiry for the purpose of increasing knowledge about and the understanding of higher education to enhance policy and practice." Within the American Educational Research Association the field is institutionalized as Division J, "Postsecondary Education," which the association states "focuses on scholars, professionals, and students who study postsecondary issues such as higher education organizations, policy, college student experiences and transitions, and university curricular issues." Its object of study is grouped in the Universal Decimal Classification under UDC 378, "Higher education. Universities. Academic study."

label: Special Education
summary: Special education is the field concerned with the education of children whose needs differ from the typical to a degree requiring adapted instruction. Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as "the education of children who differ socially, mentally, or physically from the average to such an extent that they require modifications of usual school practices," serving "children with emotional, behavioral, or cognitive impairments or with intellectual, hearing, vision, speech, or learning disabilities; gifted children with advanced academic abilities; and children with orthopedic or neurological impairments." The principal learned body in the field, the Council for Exceptional Children (CEC), describes itself as a "professional organization dedicated to improving the success of children and youth with disabilities and/or gifts and talents." In the Universal Decimal Classification the field is grouped under UDC 376, "Education, teaching, training of special groups of persons. Special schools."

label: Constitutional Law
summary: Constitutional law is the branch of law governing the basic structure and powers of the state and the fundamental rights of individuals within it. Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as "the body of rules, doctrines, and practices that govern the operation of political communities," noting that "Modern constitutional law is the offspring of nationalism as well as of the idea that the state must protect certain fundamental rights of the individual." Britannica adds that "A political community's constitution articulates the principles determining the institutions to which the task of governing is entrusted, along with their respective powers." In the Universal Decimal Classification the field falls under UDC 342, captioned "Public law. Constitutional law. Administrative law," within the law class (UDC 34, "Law. Jurisprudence").

label: International Law
summary: International law is the branch of law governing relations between states and other entities recognized as actors on the international plane. Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as "the body of legal rules, norms, and standards that apply between sovereign states and other entities that are legally recognized as international actors," noting that "The term was coined by the English philosopher Jeremy Bentham." The American Society of International Law (ASIL) states that its mission "is to foster the study of international law and to promote the establishment and maintenance of international relations on the basis of law and justice," describing itself as an organization "founded in 1906 and chartered by Congress in 1950." In the Universal Decimal Classification the field falls under UDC 341, "International law," within the law class (UDC 34, "Law. Jurisprudence").

label: Criminal Law
summary: Criminal law is the branch of law concerned with offenses against the public and the punishment of those who commit them. Encyclopaedia Britannica defines it as "the body of law that defines criminal offenses, regulates the apprehension, charging, and trial of suspected persons, and fixes penalties and modes of treatment applicable to convicted offenders." Britannica situates it as "only one of the devices by which organized societies protect the security of individual interests and ensure the survival of the group," and notes that the line between criminal law and tort law "is difficult to draw with real precision." In the Universal Decimal Classification the field falls under UDC 343, "Criminal law. Penal offences," within the law class (UDC 34, "Law. Jurisprudence").

label: Civil Law
summary: Civil law, in the branch-of-law sense, is the body of law governing non-criminal legal relationships between persons, as distinct from criminal law and from public law. Encyclopaedia Britannica characterizes private law, the broader category to which this branch belongs, as "private law regulating the actions, interests, and obligations of private persons." In the Universal Decimal Classification the branch is grouped under UDC 347, captioned "Civil law," whose own subdivisions enumerate its subject matter: 347.2 "Law of realty. Real rights" (property), 347.4 "Commitments. Contractual liabilities. Bonds. Contracts," 347.5 "Noncontractual liabilities. Torts," and 347.6 "Family law. Law of inheritance." UDC 347 sits alongside UDC 341 "International law," 342 "Public law. Constitutional law," and 343 "Criminal law" within the law class (UDC 34, "Law. Jurisprudence"). This referent is the substantive branch of private law, not a national or continental legal system.

label: Cultural Anthropology
summary: Cultural anthropology is one of the principal subfields of anthropology, concerned with human culture, social organization, and ways of life. The American Anthropological Association states that "Anthropology is the study of what makes us human," drawing "upon knowledge from the social and biological sciences as well as the humanities and physical sciences," and identifies "these four fields—human biology, archaeology, cultural anthropology, and linguistics—" as "the pillars on which the whole discipline rests." The Society for Cultural Anthropology, which describes itself as "a section of the American Anthropological Association," was "Founded in the 1980s to highlight a concern for culture and to foster interdisciplinary connections." In the Universal Decimal Classification the field is captioned "39 Cultural anthropology. Ethnography. Customs. Manners. Traditions. Way of life."

label: Economic Geography
summary: Economic geography works at the interface of economics and geography, studying the spatial distribution of economic activity. Encyclopaedia Britannica treats it within geography's human-geography branch, observing that "Economic geography has a long pedigree" and that "Its traditional focus has been the distribution of various productive activities--with subdivisions into, for example, the geography of agriculture, industrial geography, and the geography of services--and patterns of trade such as transport geography." The scholarly journal Economic Geography describes its remit as research that "deepens the understanding of geographical drivers and implications of economic processes on the economy and society." In the Universal Decimal Classification the cognate area of "Regional economics. Territorial economics" appears at UDC 332, within the economics class UDC 33.

label: Civil Engineering
summary: Civil engineering is the engineering discipline concerned with the design, construction, and maintenance of the built environment and public infrastructure. The American Society of Civil Engineers describes civil engineers as professionals who "design, build, and maintain the foundation for our modern society – our buildings, roads and bridges, drinking water and energy systems, sea ports and airports, and the infrastructure for a cleaner environment." Practitioners typically specialize within the field, with recognized technical areas including structural, geotechnical, transportation, hydraulic, environmental, and construction engineering, as well as surveying. In the Library of Congress Classification, civil engineering is treated as a general engineering domain under the heading "Technology--Engineering (General). Civil engineering (General)." The field combines applied mechanics, materials science, and project management to deliver large-scale public works that serve communities over long operational lifespans.

label: Electrical Engineering
summary: Electrical engineering is an engineering discipline concerned with the study, design, and application of equipment, devices, and systems that use electricity, electronics, and electromagnetism. It emerged as an identifiable occupation in the latter half of the 19th century after the commercialization of the electric telegraph, the telephone, and electrical power generation, distribution, and use. The field is the parent discipline for a range of subfields, including telecommunications, computer engineering, power systems, control, signal processing, and photonics. Practitioners work across scales from microelectronic circuits and integrated devices to continent-spanning power grids and communication networks. In the Library of Congress Classification, electrical engineering, electronics, and nuclear engineering are grouped under class TK.

label: Mechanical Engineering
summary: Mechanical engineering is an engineering branch concerned with physical machines and mechanisms involving force and movement. It combines engineering physics and mathematics with materials science to design, analyze, manufacture, and maintain mechanical systems, and is one of the oldest and broadest engineering branches. Core subject areas include mechanics, dynamics, thermodynamics, materials science, structural analysis, and design. The Library of Congress Classification places the discipline in range TJ1-TJ1570, captioned "Mechanical engineering and machinery." The American Society of Mechanical Engineers, founded in 1880, is the field's principal professional body; ASME states that its mission "is to advance engineering for the benefit of humanity."

label: Chemical Engineering
summary: Chemical engineering is an engineering field which deals with the study of the operation and design of chemical plants as well as methods of improving production. Practitioners develop practical commercial processes that transform raw materials into marketable products, integrating principles from chemistry, physics, mathematics, biology, and economics to manage energy and material transformations efficiently. Work ranges from small-scale laboratory study of nanomaterials to massive industrial operations. Core responsibilities include safety evaluations, process optimization, system modeling, reaction engineering, and operational guidelines for manufacturing facilities. The discipline is organized around unit operations and process design, scaling chemical and physical changes from the laboratory to continuous industrial production.

label: Materials Science and Engineering
summary: Materials science is an interdisciplinary field concerned with understanding the relationships between the structure of materials and their properties and using this knowledge to design materials for specific applications. The internal structure of a material—from atomic arrangements to microscopic features—strongly influences its mechanical, electrical, thermal, and optical behavior. In engineering practice, materials science and engineering are often described through the processing–structure–properties–performance paradigm, in which processing determines structure, structure determines properties, and properties ultimately control the performance of a material in service. The combined discipline therefore unites a scientific dimension, investigating why materials behave as they do, with an engineering dimension, producing and selecting materials for components and devices. Major material classes studied include metals, ceramics, polymers, semiconductors, and composites.

label: Environmental Engineering
summary: Environmental engineering is a professional engineering discipline related to environmental science. It encompasses broad scientific topics like chemistry, biology, ecology, geology, hydraulics, hydrology, microbiology, and mathematics to create solutions that will protect and also improve the health of living organisms and improve the quality of the environment. The field has historical roots in sanitary engineering and is regarded as a sub-discipline of civil engineering and chemical engineering. Typical work addresses water and wastewater treatment, air pollution control, solid and hazardous waste management, and the remediation of contaminated sites. Environmental engineers design systems and infrastructure that limit the discharge of pollutants and safeguard public health, distinguishing the discipline from environmental science, which centers on studying environmental processes rather than engineering solutions.

label: Aerospace Engineering
summary: Aerospace engineering is the primary field of engineering concerned with the development of aircraft and spacecraft. It has two major and overlapping branches, aeronautical engineering and astronautical engineering, while avionics engineering deals with the electronics side of the field. As an application of mechanical-engineering principles to flight vehicles, it draws on aerodynamics, propulsion, structures, and control. The Library of Congress Classification places aeronautics within range TL500-TL778, captioned "Aeronautics. Aeronautical engineering," inside the broader class TL1-TL4050, "Motor vehicles. Aeronautics. Astronautics." The American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics, formed in 1963 by the merger of the American Rocket Society and the Institute of the Aerospace Sciences, is described as "the world's largest technical society dedicated to the global aerospace profession."

label: Industrial Engineering
summary: Industrial engineering is concerned with the design, improvement and installation of integrated systems of people, materials, information, equipment and energy. It draws upon specialized knowledge and skill in the mathematical, physical, and social sciences together with the principles and methods of engineering analysis and design, to specify, predict, and evaluate the results to be obtained from such systems. The branch focuses on optimizing complex processes, systems, and organizations by improving efficiency, productivity, and quality. Industrial engineers aim to reduce waste, streamline operations, and enhance overall performance across many industries; the Institute of Industrial and Systems Engineers notes that "Industrial and systems engineers make things better in any industry – from automobile manufacturing and aerospace, to healthcare, forestry, finance, leisure, and education."

label: Biotechnology
summary: Biotechnology is a multidisciplinary field that involves the integration of natural sciences and engineering sciences to achieve the application of organisms and parts thereof for products and services. Specialists in the field are known as biotechnologists. The discipline draws on biology, chemistry, and engineering to harness living systems, cells, and biomolecules in manufacturing and process development. Applications include the production of pharmaceuticals, enzymes, biofuels, and agricultural and food products, as well as industrial processes that use microorganisms or enzymes in place of conventional chemical synthesis. As an engineering and technology field, biotechnology emphasizes the design, scale-up, and control of biological processes to deliver marketable products and services, complementing the basic life sciences that supply its underlying knowledge.

label: Structural Engineering
summary: Structural engineering is a sub-discipline of civil engineering concerned with the analysis and design of structures that must safely support or resist loads. Wikipedia characterizes it as the field "in which structural engineers are trained to design the 'bones and joints' that create the form and shape of human-made structures," adding that engineers "must understand and calculate the stability, strength, rigidity and earthquake-susceptibility of built structures for buildings and nonbuilding structures." The discipline rests on applied physical laws and empirical knowledge of how different materials and geometries perform under stress. Typical work covers buildings, bridges, towers, and other load-bearing systems, ensuring they withstand gravity, wind, seismic, and service loads. The Library of Congress Classification gives structural engineering its own heading, "Structural engineering (General)," within the broader civil engineering range.

label: Geotechnical Engineering
summary: Geotechnical engineering is the branch of civil engineering concerned with the engineering behavior of earth materials. Wikipedia defines it, "also known as geotechnics," as "the branch of civil engineering concerned with the engineering behavior of earth materials." The discipline applies principles of soil mechanics and rock mechanics to investigate subsurface conditions and to design foundations, retaining structures, slopes, embankments, and tunnels. ASCE's Geo-Institute, the field's professional home, describes itself as "a community of geoprofessionals advancing geotechnical engineering" whose members "work to improve infrastructure, reduce risk, and ensure safe, resilient communities." The Library of Congress Classification places the related body of knowledge under "Engineering geology" within civil engineering. Practitioners assess how soils and rock respond to loading, water, and excavation, providing the geotechnical basis on which surface structures and earthworks depend.

label: Transportation Engineering
summary: Transportation engineering is the sub-discipline of civil engineering that applies scientific and engineering principles to the planning, design, operation, and management of transportation systems. Wikipedia defines it as "the application of technology and scientific principles to the planning, functional design, operation and management of facilities for any mode of transportation to provide for the safe, efficient, rapid, comfortable, convenient, economical, and environmentally compatible movement of people and goods." The field spans highway, rail, transit, air, water, and pipeline modes. ASCE's Transportation & Development Institute, established in 2002, is dedicated to "advancing knowledge and practice in sustainable transportation and development." The Library of Congress Classification recognizes the discipline under the heading "Transportation engineering" within civil engineering.
